## pqac-00000035

From text 'dankhazi2015ebsdsamplepreparation pages 3-6'.

Zoltán Dankházi, Szilvia Kalácska, Adrienn Baris, Gábor Varga, Zsolt Radi, and Károly Havancsák. Ebsd sample preparation: high energy ar ion milling. Materials Science Forum, 812:309-314, Feb 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.4028/www.scientific.net/msf.812.309, doi:10.4028/www.scientific.net/msf.812.309. This article has 9 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt supports a comparison in which planar, shallow-angle broad Ar-ion milling is advantageous for preparing an existing roughly polished surface for high-quality EBSD. At approximately 6–8° incidence, it removes the mechanically deformed or amorphous surface layer, improves EBSD image quality, and requires relatively short treatment times; for Cu, the recommended duration is 6–8 minutes, with material-dependent values listed for Al, Ni, Fe, and steel. Milling should stop near the beginning of IQ saturation because extended processing causes surface coarsening, roughness, and potentially cratering, which are disadvantages for both EBSD quality and surface-sensitive EDS. Cross-section or slope-cut mode is advantageous when the original surface contains a thick mechanically induced amorphous layer that planar polishing cannot readily remove, or when a newly exposed subsurface is needed. It can produce a substantial section (up to 200 µm depth in 2 hours), enabling examination of internal structure. However, cross-section milling is slower and high-energy cutting generates redeposited/backsputtered material that forms an amorphous layer and blurs Kikuchi patterns. A subsequent low-energy Ar cleaning step was required to obtain a usable EBSD map. The excerpt does not directly discuss EDS performance, but the reported roughening, redeposition, and surface-layer effects would also be relevant to EDS accuracy and spatial resolution.

From text 'gauzzi2020electronbackscatterdiffraction pages 7-9'.

T Gauzzi, MCC de Souza, and GC Stumpf. Electron backscatter diffraction (ebsd) sample preparation revisited: integrating traditional methods and new techniques in the last three decades. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt provides general information about ion milling and distinguishes the development of cross-section polishers from conventional broad ion-beam milling, but it does not directly compare planar (flat) broad-beam mode with cross-section mode, nor does it specifically discuss EDS performance. For EBSD preparation, ion milling is described as advantageous because it avoids residues associated with colloidal-silica polishing and can produce better-quality, high-resolution Kikuchi patterns. The method requires careful adjustment of ion-beam voltage, incidence angle, sample movement, milling duration, and other conditions according to the material. Examples show that broad milling polishers can be used with varied parameter sequences, including different tilt angles and voltages for roughing and finishing. Cross-section polishers are identified as newer equipment developed specifically for SEM and EBSD and applied to diverse materials. The excerpt therefore supports evaluating each mode based on surface quality, material type, geometry, and parameter control, but it supplies no explicit advantages or disadvantages concerning flat-area coverage, exposed subsurface regions, curtaining, redeposition, specimen thickness, compositional artifacts, or EDS accuracy. Those specific planar-versus-cross-section comparisons would require additional source material.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.micron.2022.103268, doi:10.1016/j.micron.2022.103268. This article has 22 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly supports the benefits of planar/flat BIB preparation for EBSD: it is intended to produce a flat, preparation-artifact-free surface, can process large areas, may replace substantial mechanical polishing, and can reduce preparation damage relative to mechanical methods. These characteristics are also potentially beneficial for surface-sensitive EDS, although EDS-specific performance is not discussed in the excerpt. The text identifies key disadvantages and trade-offs of BIB generally: ion milling can introduce radiation damage, point defects, implantation, phase transformations, and defect clustering; higher accelerating voltage increases sputtering but can increase ion implantation and knock-on damage. Near-parallel polishing angles reduce direct implantation but may produce shadowing, curtaining, and periodic ripple roughness, especially with prior surface roughness or extended polishing. Cross-section mode is mentioned only as a destructive 3D sectioning approach, which can enable large-area three-dimensional analysis and high indexing rates. However, the excerpt does not provide a direct comparison of planar versus cross-section geometry, nor does it discuss EDS signal geometry, redeposition, trench walls, or accessibility of subsurface interfaces. Thus, it offers general guidance on BIB benefits and artifacts but insufficient evidence for a complete mode-by-mode comparison.

This article has 168 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides a limited comparison between broad ion beam (BIB) thinning and FIB cross-section milling that is relevant to EBSD and EDS specimen preparation. BIB final milling generally uses a larger incidence geometry (approximately 3–15°) than FIB final milling (approximately 1–5°), and compositional differences in sputtering yield naturally generate surface roughness during BIB thinning. This roughness can be disadvantageous for surface-sensitive analyses such as EBSD and may also complicate EDS interpretation through topographic and redeposition effects. In contrast, FIB cross-sectioning is described as producing uniform, large cross sections more steadily than BIB thinning and permitting the cross-section position to be selected. FIB also offers better positional control, although its accuracy is limited by beam size and can be on the order of tens of nanometers. The excerpt emphasizes that FIB cross sections require tilt correction for a truly vertical section and uniform TEM thickness, while BIB does not permit positioning the thinning surface at a specific location. It does not directly discuss EBSD pattern quality, EDS signal geometry, detector shadowing, contamination, or damage-layer thickness, so those specific comparisons cannot be established from this passage alone.

T Gauzzi, MCC de Souza, and GC Stumpf. Electron backscatter diffraction (ebsd) sample preparation revisited: integrating traditional methods and new techniques in the last three decades. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt does not directly compare planar (flat) broad ion-beam milling with cross-section mode, nor does it explicitly discuss EDS-specific advantages or disadvantages. It does indicate that ion milling can be preferable to colloidal-silica mechanical polishing because it leaves no residues, can produce better high-resolution Kikuchi patterns, and is less hazardous and complex than electropolishing. Cross-section polishers and other dedicated ion-mill systems were developed for SEM/EBSD preparation and have produced good results across many materials. Their performance depends strongly on accelerating voltage, beam angle, sample movement, milling time, and material type; therefore, parameters must be optimized for each specimen. Examples show that different materials require substantially different milling durations and angles, and that multistep procedures may be needed to obtain the best surface. For a planar versus cross-section comparison, the excerpt supports only the general point that cross-section equipment enables preparation of sectioned surfaces and that ion-beam conditions must be carefully controlled. ## pqac-00000041

From text 'ajantiwalay2019bestpracticesfor pages 5-7'.

Tanvi Ajantiwalay, Tammy Trowbridge, Alexander Winston, Cheng Sun, Kumar Sridharan, and Assel Aitkaliyeva. Best practices for preparing radioactive specimens for ebsd analysis. Micron, 118:1-8, Mar 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.micron.2018.12.002, doi:10.1016/j.micron.2018.12.002. This article has 11 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt supports that silica residue from vibratory/metallographic polishing can remain trapped in pores and interfere with EBSD analysis: the authors report that silica particles left in pores caused poor indexing, even though the polished surface was otherwise adequate for pore-size-distribution measurements. The text also establishes that ion milling, particularly FIB milling, can produce surface artifacts and microstructural changes. These include implanted or damaged surface material, curtaining/streaking, and apparent coalescence or growth of pores. However, the excerpt does not specifically state that ion milling redeposits trapped silica onto surrounding surfaces, nor does it directly demonstrate that milled silica residue creates artifacts on adjacent surfaces. It only provides the broader evidence that ion-beam processing can damage or implant material and generate milling-related artifacts. Therefore, the reported silica entrapment is supported for polishing, while redeposition and its effects on neighboring surfaces remain unconfirmed by this passage.

is obvious that this resolution cannot be obtained by visible light and neutrons cannot
be focused sufﬁciently to a small spot size. X-rays can, in fact, be focused (there exists
a technique called µ-XRF), but particle accelerators are needed to produce X-rays for
this technique. Typically, a larger volume of the specimen is radiated with neutrons and
with X-ray photons, meaning that while macrotexture analysis can be performed, we
get no information on the microtexture. We shall use electrons then: they can easily be

                                  1KITTI RATTER                                        1  INTRODUCTION


focused to a very small spot size using electromagnets and they can diffract like phonons
or neutrons [1].
   The history of the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) started when Kikuchi and
his supervisor discovered the electron diffraction pattern, later named after Kikuchi,
in 1928 [2]. They were using a 50 keV electron beam on a thin mica ﬁlm, and the
diffraction patterns were recorded by photographic plates. The discovery started an
avalanche of work on electron diffraction, and many ended up studying the transmitted
as well as the reﬂected electron diffraction patterns on a large number of materials in
different conﬁgurations: see Boersch (1937) [3] and Alam (1954) [4].  In 1965 the
ﬁrst commercial SEM appeared on the market, which allowed even faster progress.
Venables and Harland were the ﬁrst to investigate electron backscatter Kikuchi patterns
using SEM. In the beginning patterns were detected by a TV camera and later by a
phosphorous screen [5]. In 1984 Venables work was continued by Digley, who added
the help of a computer for indexing the patterns [6], which proved a major step in the
success of modern-day EBSD.
   The system which scientists use now dates back to 1993, when Brent Adams in-
troduced the term orientation mapping (OM). Orientation mapping uses the operating
principle of the SEM, namely, a well focused electron beam is scanning the surface of
the sample and products are being collected and being displayed at each point. The
products in this case are diffraction patterns produced by backscattered electrons, which
are indexed automatically by the computer, resulting in colour being displayed on the
screen according to the orientation of the grain found at that speciﬁc point of the speci-
men [7].
   The EBSD technique is a very young technique and a very challenging one in that
sense that it requires major computing capacity, or before that was available, major
human power for the indexing of each pattern. Just for the sake of comparison, using
the ﬁrst computer-aided indexing, the operator had to select three lines at each pattern,
before the indexing could be done by the computer. The orientation maps to be shown
in this work consist of 200   200 = 40000 points.  If we assume indexing one point               ×
takes 5 seconds on average, one map would take 200000 seconds = 56 hours to produce.
These days we are lucky in that powerful computers and well written algorithms are
available to reduce the duration of one mapping (as mentioned above) to less than 15
minutes. However, we should remember that what we can do now by just one click,

                                  2KITTI RATTER                                        1  INTRODUCTION


others worked for for years (not only in the case of EBSD).
   The crucial part of the sample for the purpose of the EBSD investigation is the
surface, since the information we get comes from the upper 10 nanometer thick region
of the specimen. The surface has to be perfectly clean, there cannot be an amorphous
covering on it. If there is, either no or a faded diffraction pattern is recorded. Besides,
it has to be effectively smoothed, because of shadowing effects. The usual diamond
polishing is out of the question, because it can deform the grains on top and this induced
stress causes the diffuseness of the diffraction patterns. It has been suggested to polish
with colloidal silica for hours. When we attempted this, we could ﬁnd residual polishing
material in the grains of the sample. We also tried to prepare the surface using electro-
polishing, but we were unable to see any Kikuchi bands.
   The requirements for surface quality is very similar to what is expected in the case
of a transmission electron microscopy sample, the difference being that only one side of
the specimen is important. This similarity gave us the idea to try a device that has proven
trustworthy when preparing TEM samples: the Gentle Mill low enery argon ion polisher.
This instrument was purposely designed for the ﬁnal polishing of TEM samples by an
internationally successful company, Technoorg Linda Ltd. Co. They provided us with
an instrument to try its qualities in this area and if successful, preparing a protocol for
fast surface preparation.
   Besides probing the properties of Gentle Mill, we also used the built-in focused ion
beam system in our microscope. One of the reasons for this was that after surface prepa-
ration with the Gentle Mill, the sample had to be moved from instrument to instrument.
There can be sensitive samples that do not prefer to be transferred. With an efﬁcient
protocol, these samples can be prepared inside the microscope chamber and only stage
movements are required before the EBSD investigation can take place.
   This work is divided into two parts. In the ﬁrst part, the instruments and the meth-
ods are described. Staring with an introduction to the scanning electron microscopes
and focused ion beam systems, pointing out the speciﬁcations of our system.  In the
following chapter, the working principle of the Gentle Mill is described, then a sim-
ple model for ion sputtering is given. After the instrument descriptions, the theory of
electron backscatter diffraction is reviewed, ﬁrst with the kinematical theory, then, after
realizing that this approximation is not valid, the main ideas of dynamic theory are ex-
plained. When the theory is understood, we turn to the actual instrumentation of EBSD

                                  3KITTI RATTER                                        1  INTRODUCTION


and the details of representing the orientation information.
    In the second part, our measurements and results are discussed, starting with the
data where FIB was used and ﬁnishing with those where Gentle Mill was employed.
The conclusion points out our main results and plots our plans for the future.

2  Methods and Equipment

   The measurements and sample preparation described in this thesis were performed
in the Department of Materials Physics at Eötvös University using a FEI Quanta 3D
FEG dual-beam scanning electron microscope (ﬁgure 1) and a Gentle Mill 3 low energy
ion polisher provided by Technoorg Linda Ltd. Co. (ﬁgure 2).

2.1  FEI Quanta 3D FEG Dual-Beam Scanning Electron Microscope

    In dual-beam electron microscopes, besides the electron source there is an ion source
as well. Both beams are suitable for imaging the surface of the sample, but the ion beam
is typically used for sputtering or milling. A schematic diagram of a scanning electron
microscope can be seen in ﬁgure 3.
   The electron beam is produced by thermionic ﬁeld emission (Schottky emission)
from a tungsten needle coated with zirconium dioxide (ZrO2) and is then accelerated to
an energy chosen by the user (2 keV -30 keV ) by an electric ﬁeld, before being focused
by condenser lenses to a spot on the specimen. The diameter of the beam as measured on
the sample is about 1 nm, depending on the voltage, current and the time elapsed since
the last adjustment. The beam passes through pairs of scanning coils, which deﬂect
the beam in the x-y plane so that it scans in a raster fashion over a rectangular area of

and formed must be under high vacuum (10−7 Pa). In conventional scanning electron

Abstract:
Cooling Rate (CR) definitively influences the microstructure of metallic parts manufactured through various processes. Factors including cooling medium, surface area, thermal conductivity, and temperature control can influence both predicted and unforeseen impacts that then influence the results of mechanical properties. This comprehensive study explores the impact of CRs in diffusion, microstructural development, and the characterization of aluminum alloys and the influence of various manufacturing processes and post-process treatments, and it studies analytical models that can predict their effects. It examines a broad range of CRs encountered in diverse manufacturing methods, such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), directed energy deposition (DED), casting, forging, welding, and hot isostatic pressing (HIP). For example, varying CRs might result in different types of solidification and microstructural evolution in aluminum alloys, which thereby influence their mechanical properties during end use. The study further examines the effects of post-process heat treatments, including quenching, annealing, and precipitation hardening, on the microstructure and mechanical properties of aluminum alloys. It discusses numerical and analytical models, which are used to predict and optimize CRs for achieving targeted material characteristics of specific aluminum alloys. Although understanding CR and its effects is crucial, there is a lack of literature on how CR affects alloy properties. This comprehensive review aims to bridge the knowledge gap through a thorough literature review of the impact of CR on microstructure and mechanical properties.

messages.content: Now let me create the summary artifact:

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a summary table for all 9 assumptions in the metallographic preparation plan review. For each numbered assumption, include columns for: Assumption number, Brief description, Verdict (Supported/Contradicted/Silent/Partially supported), Key evidence summary, and Risk level (Low/Medium/High/Critical). Include these findings:

1. Ion milling removes silica residue so abrasive choice doesn't matter → Partially supported. Ion milling avoids residues but no direct test that it removes pre-existing CS films for EDS equivalence. Rémond 2002 shows CS polishing affects Al Kα ratios at 5 keV (1.058 vs ~0.970 for diamond polish). Risk: Medium.

2. Cleaning before milling is optional → Contradicted. Surface contamination and scratches can cause roughening, charging artifacts, and cone formation during milling. Barber 1993, Ajantiwalay 2019. Risk: Medium.

3. Silica in pores doesn't contaminate surrounding surface → Partially supported. Silica trapped in pores confirmed (Ajantiwalay 2019). No direct evidence it is redeposited by ion milling onto flat areas. But ion milling CAN cause redeposition. Risk: Medium.

4. Differential sputtering creates only minor relief → Partially supported with caution. Preferential sputtering of multiphase alloys is well-documented (Barber 1993, Nowak 2021, Ulitschka 2020). Extended milling causes surface coarsening (Dankházi 2015). Al and Si have different sputtering yields. But short finishing steps at low angle minimize relief. Risk: Medium.

5. Ar implantation and damage do not bias EDS/EBSD → Supported. Damage layer is a few nm at 4-5 kV. EBSD quality generally improved by low-energy ion milling. EDS interaction volume at 5-15 kV much deeper. Risk: Low.

6. Beam heating doesn't alter microstructure; phenolic mount OK → CONTRADICTED. Specimen temperatures can reach 400°C during 5 kV Ar milling (Viguier 2001). DSC onset for Si precipitation ~185°C (Bosio 2021). Phenolic mount outgassing is a known issue. Risk: CRITICAL.

7. 5 h vibratory step could be skipped → Partially supported. Deformation layer 1-100 nm from 1 μm polishing. Ion milling can remove it in minutes. But longer milling increases heating risk. AA7021 study used electropolishing first. Risk: Medium.

8. Native oxide adds negligible O to 5 kV EDS → Partially supported with caution. Native Al oxide is 2-5 nm. At 5 kV, interaction volume ~200-400 nm, but oxide is proportionally significant. Rémond 2002 shows energy-dependent k-ratio variations. Risk: Medium.

9. Planar milling better than cross-section mode → Supported. Larger area, preserves geometry, faster. Cross-section has more redeposition, requires cleaning (Dankházi 2015). Risk: Low."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Assumption | Brief description | Verdict | Key evidence summary | Risk |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ion milling removes silica residue and deformation, making the final abrasive irrelevant to EDS. | **Partially supported** | Ion milling can provide a residue-free finish, but no retrieved study demonstrates complete removal of a pre-existing close-packed colloidal-silica film or equivalence of silica- and alumina-polished Al after milling. Final polishing can affect low-voltage X-ray intensities: for polycrystalline alumina, the Al Kα ratio after colloidal-silica polishing was **1.058 at 5 keV**, versus **0.970** after 0.25 µm diamond polishing; differences largely diminished by 15–25 keV. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000016) | **Medium** |
| 2 | Cleaning before ion milling is optional because particles and films do not produce milling artifacts. | **Contradicted** | Initial scratches, topography, contamination, and foreign sites can promote roughening, charging-related deflection, curtaining, craters, cones, and other ion-milling topography. Silica residues can also impair EBSD indexing. The 2 min water polish is therefore not proven uniquely effective, but removal of loose residue before milling is not optional in principle. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024) | **Medium** |
| 3 | Silica trapped in pores remains there and is not redeposited onto surrounding material. | **Partially supported** | Silica entrapment in pores is documented and can cause poor EBSD indexing. No retrieved publication directly demonstrates redistribution of pore-trapped silica onto adjacent Al during broad-beam milling; however, sputtered-material redeposition is a recognized ion-milling mechanism, so avoiding EDS spots near pores does not by itself exclude contamination of nearby surfaces. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000041) | **Medium** |
| 4 | Differential sputtering of eutectic Si and α-Al creates only minor relief without analytical consequences. | **Partially supported** | Preferential sputtering and orientation- or phase-dependent erosion in multiphase alloys are well documented; precipitates can protrude, form pits, or become non-indexable, and extended milling can coarsen or roughen a surface. Low incidence, rotation, short endpoint-controlled milling, and stopping when EBSD IQ saturates mitigate—but do not eliminate—the risk. No retrieved study quantified the resulting EDS bias specifically for LPBF AlSi10Mg. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000042) | **Medium** |
| 5 | Ar implantation and a few-nanometre damage layer do not materially bias EDS or EBSD. | **Supported** | Low-energy Ar finishing is widely used to improve EBSD by removing the mechanically deformed layer. Its shallow altered layer is small relative to the bulk X-ray generation depth at 5–15 kV, so major-element EDS bias is unlikely. Nevertheless, direct Al-specific measurements of implanted Ar and quantitative low-kV EDS bias were not found, and EBSD remains intrinsically sensitive to the upper approximately 10 nm. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000044) | **Low** |
| 6 | A 25 min, 5/4 kV mill cannot alter as-built AlSi10Mg; cooling and mount qualification are unnecessary. | **Contradicted** | Aluminum-alloy specimens reached as high as **673 K ≈ 400 °C** during 5 kV Ar milling; holder/contact design changed measured temperatures by roughly 100–200 K. LPBF AlSi10Mg-based material shows a precipitation-related DSC event beginning near **185 °C**, while clear Si rejection/coarsening is reported above roughly **275 °C**. Thus an unmeasured stage temperature cannot be presumed safe. The retrieved literature did not validate ordinary phenolic Bakelite for this mill; resin outgassing, poor thermal contact, charging, and local heating require instrument-specific qualification. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048) | **Critical** |
| 7 | The 5 h vibratory step can be omitted and ion milling can start after 1 µm alumina or CAMI 1200 SiC. | **Partially supported** | Mechanically produced amorphous/deformed layers are reported at approximately **1–100 nm**, and optimized shallow-angle Ar milling can remove such layers in minutes for some metals. That does not validate **20–25 min at 4–5 kV** after 1 µm alumina—or especially after 1200 SiC—for AlSi10Mg. Milling time is material-specific, residual scratches may persist, and longer milling increases heating and relief risks. The cited AA7021 route also included electropolishing, so it is not evidence for ion milling directly after coarse preparation. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000042) | **Medium** |
| 8 | Native-oxide regrowth during prompt transfer adds negligible O to 5 kV EDS. | **Partially supported** | Air-exposed Al rapidly forms a self-limiting oxide/contamination film commonly about **2–5 nm** thick. This is small relative to the overall 5 kV interaction volume, but O Kα is a surface-sensitive light-element signal and the oxide occupies a non-negligible fraction of the shallow X-ray-generating region. Prompt, standardized transfer improves repeatability but does not make measured oxygen a bulk value or separate oxide O from pore/residue O. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000014) | **Medium** |
| 9 | Planar milling is preferable to the tool’s cross-section mode for same-face EDS and EBSD. | **Supported** | Planar milling preserves the existing section plane, offers the stated approximately 2 mm field, and efficiently removes near-surface deformation. Cross-section mode avoids abrasive contact and is valuable as an independent control, but provides a narrower face and can introduce redeposition/backsputtered amorphous material requiring a final cleaning step. Planar mode is preferable for routine same-face correlation once heating and relief are controlled; cross-section mode is the stronger validation route for preparation contamination. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038) | **Low** |


*Table: Literature-based verdicts for the nine preparation assumptions, with quantitative evidence and practical risk rankings. The dominant concern is unmeasured ion-beam heating of metastable as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg.*

Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer: [artifact-00]

Context IDs that may be cited: [pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051]

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

Usage:

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Rubber-duck review of a metallographic preparation plan. Please challenge it. For each numbered assumption below, say whether the published literature supports it, contradicts it, or is silent, with citations and numbers where available. Then name the biggest risk we have not considered, and the smallest experiment that would test it.

Context. Material: laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) AlSi10Mg in the as-built condition (fine cellular eutectic Si network, Si-supersaturated Al, some gas and lack-of-fusion pores); later, other Al alloys, some of them Si-free. Goals: quantitative SEM-EDS at 5-15 kV (Al, Si, Mg, O and minor elements) and EBSD on the same polished face. Equipment: a rotary grinder/polisher, a Buehler VibroMet 2 vibratory polisher, and a JEOL IB-19530CP-type broad argon-ion "cross section polisher" that is also used for planar (flat) surface milling of an area about 2 mm across. Samples are ~1 cm pieces hot-mounted in phenolic (Bakelite).

Current plan: SiC paper 320, 400, 600, 800, 1200 (US CAMI grades) -> 1 um alumina on a flock cloth -> 0.05 um alkaline colloidal silica on the VibroMet 2 for about 5 h -> 2 min on a clean soft pad with distilled water only at 40 rpm -> rinse, ethanol/methanol, dry -> broad-beam Ar ion planar milling (copying a recent study on AA7021 sheet: 5 kV for 20 min, then 4 kV for 5 min) -> SEM-EDS and EBSD.

Assumptions to test:
1. Ion milling after the silica step removes both the colloidal-silica residue (an earlier sample carried a close-packed film of ~40 nm silica spheres) and the residual deformation layer, so the choice of final abrasive (colloidal silica vs 0.05 um alumina) no longer matters for EDS accuracy.
2. Particles or films left on the surface before milling do not cause milling artifacts (masking, cones, ripples), so cleaning before milling (the 2 min water polish, per Maleki et al. 2023, Additive Manufacturing Letters 5:100122) is optional once milling is used.
3. Silica trapped in pores is not removed by milling but is not redeposited onto the surrounding surface either; keeping EDS spots away from pores is enough.
4. Differential sputtering of eutectic Si versus the alpha-Al matrix under 4-6 kV Ar ions at low incidence angle produces only minor relief that does not bias EDS quantification at 5-15 kV or degrade EBSD.
5. Ar implantation and ion damage (a few nm) do not bias EDS and do not significantly reduce EBSD pattern quality on aluminum.
6. Beam heating during ~25 min of milling at 5 kV does not alter the metastable as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure (Si precipitation from supersaturated Al, coarsening or spheroidization of the Si network), so a cooled stage is unnecessary. The phenolic mount is not a problem in the mill (outgassing, charging, heating).
7. The 5 h vibratory step could be skipped: going from 1 um alumina (or even from SiC 1200) straight to ion milling would still give EBSD-quality, residue-free surfaces, because 20-25 min of 4-5 kV planar milling removes the deformed layer left by 1 um alumina on Al-Si. (The AA7021 study also electropolished for 30 s before milling.)
8. After milling, native-oxide regrowth during transfer to the SEM adds negligible O to 5 kV EDS; loading promptly is enough.
9. Planar milling of the mechanically polished face is a better route for these goals than the same tool's cross-section mode (a ~1 mm wide ion-cut face perpendicular to the mount surface, with no abrasive contact).

Also: is there any published comparison of quantitative EDS or EPMA accuracy (k-ratios, analytical totals) on ion-milled versus mechanically polished Al or Al-Si alloy surfaces?

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to systematically address each of the 9 assumptions and the additional question about EDS/EPMA comparisons on ion-milled vs mechanically polished surfaces.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The growing use of duplex stainless steels (DSSs) has spurred extensive research and development, particularly concerning weldability challenges. The increasing interest in additive manufacturing (AM) using directed energy deposition (DED) has further highlighted the need for precise sample preparation to ensure accurate microstructural characterization. This paper consolidates best practices for preparing samples to effectively reveal microstructures and secondary phases in DSSs. By optimizing polishing techniques and etching methods, the work provides guidelines for distinguishing ferrite and austenite across the base material, heat-affected zone (HAZ), and weld metal, while also enabling the detection of intermetallic phases and discrete secondary precipitates. Examples of typical deviations, etching phenomena, and potential pitfalls are also provided. The preparation strategies presented are tailored to support subsequent analysis using light optical microscopy (LOM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).</jats:p>

Abstract:
An electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) method provides information about the crystallographic structure of materials. However, a surface subjected to analysis needs to be well-prepared. This usually requires following a time-consuming procedure of mechanical polishing. The alternative methods of surface preparation for EBSD are performed via electropolishing or focus ion beam (FIB). In the present study, plasma etching using a glow discharge optical emission spectrometer (GD-OES) was applied for surface preparation for EBSD analysis. The obtained results revealed that plasma etching through GD-OES can be successfully used for surface preparation for EBSD analysis. However, it was also found that the plasma etching is sensitive for the alloy microstructure, i.e., the presence of intermetallic phases and precipitates such as carbides possess a different sputtering rate, resulting in non-uniform plasma etching. Preparation of the cross-section of oxidized CM247 revealed a similar problem with non-uniformity of plasma etching. The carbides and oxide scale possess a lower sputtering rate than the metallic matrix, which caused formation of relief. Based on obtained results, possible resolutions to suppress the effect of different sputtering rates are proposed.

Abstract:
Aluminum and its alloy magnetron sputtering targets, owing to their superior electrical/thermal conductivity and robust substrate adhesion, serve as critical materials in advanced electronics and information technologies. It is known that the microstructure of the target, including grain uniformity and crystallographic texture, directly affects the sputtering performance and the quality of the deposited thin film. Despite extensive research efforts, the review paper focused on the microstructure of aluminum target materials is still absent. In that context, the recent progress on the Al alloy target is reviewed, focusing on grain refinement and texture control strategies. The roles of alloying elements, such as Si, Cu, and rare-earth Sc and Nd, are described first. The two conventional manufacturing techniques of fabricating Al targets, including melting and powder metallurgy, are introduced. Then, studies on grain refinement by thermomechanical processing routes (hot/cold rolling, annealing and forging) are summarized. Lastly, texture engineering through deformation and heat treatment protocols (unidirectional/multidirectional rolling, deformation thickness, and composite deformation modes) is reviewed. By establishing the relationship between thermomechanical processing and microstructure, this review provides insights for designing high-performance aluminum targets tailored to next-generation advanced thin-film applications.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Modes de fatigue des métallisations à base d'aluminium dans les composants MOSFET de puissance</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Cette thèse, effectuée en collaboration entre le CEMES-CNRS, le laboratoire Satie (ENS Cachan) et NXP Semiconductors est motivée par la compréhension des mécanismes de défaillance des dispositifs MOSFET pour les applications dans l'industrie automobile. Un facteur limitant de la fiabilité à long terme des modules de puissance basse tension est le vieillissement électrothermique et/ou thermo-mécanique des parties métalliques de la source: métallisation en aluminium (ou alliage) et fils de connexion. A cause de la différence de coefficient de dilatation thermique entre la métallisation les oxydes et le substrat semi-conducteur, la température atteinte pendant les cycles de fonctionnement (quelques centaines de degrés), induit une déformation plastique inévitable dans le métal, qui est le matériau le plus mou dans l'architecture complexe du MOSFET. Nous avons caractérisé la microstructure métallique avant et après les tests de vieillissement électrothermique accélérés, en utilisant des techniques spécifiques du domaine de la métallurgie physique: microscopie électronique et ionique, cartographie d'orientation de grains et de la composition chimique. Pour la première fois, la métallisation de la source a été caractérisée sous les fils de connexion, qui sont cent fois plus épais que la métallisation. Cet emplacement est critique pour la fiabilité du composant, car le processus de soudure par ultrasons induit une déformation plastique importante qui peut affaiblir la métallisation initiale avant le vieillissement. Ceci est peu étudié dans la littérature en raison de la difficulté à accéder à la métallisation sous les fils sans altérer leur interface, souvent endommagée et fragilisée dans les modules vieillis. Nous avons mis en place des méthodes de préparation d'échantillon, basées sur le polissage ionique, pour étudier cette interface, sans introduire d'artefacts de préparation. Le processus de soudure à froid induit une déformation plastique sévère et non uniforme dans la métallisation sous les fils sans parvenir à recréer un bon contact électrique: de petites cavités et des résidus d'oxyde natif, ont été systématiquement observés à l'interface Al / Al, dans tous les modules analysés, avant et après vieillissement. Le mécanisme principal de défaillance des modules est la génération et la propagation de fissures de fatigue dans l'aluminium, associée à une oxydation locale qui empêche la fermeture de ces fissures. Sous et en dehors des fils de connexion, ces fissures traversent la métallisation perpendiculairement à la surface jusqu'au substrat en silicium en suivant les joints de grains. Cette fissuration est due à la diffusion intergranulaire accélérée des atomes d'aluminium. Dans la zone de soudure, le phénomène de fissuration parallèle à l'interface est favorisé par les imperfections initiales (cavités, oxyde). Les expériences de tomographie ionique ont montré que ces fissures sont confinées à l'interface fil-métal et ne se propagent pas dans le fil malgré sa plus faible résistance mécanique (Al pur, structure à grains plus grands). La propagation de la fissure le long de l'interface Al/Al peut provoquer une diminution du contact entre le fil et la métallisation de la source et éventuellement son décollement. Les fissures dans le métal source peuvent expliquer l'augmentation locale de la résistance et de la température du module qui accélère le processus de vieillissement jusqu'à l'échec. Cette étude a établi de nouvelles techniques dédiées et des méthodes de quantification pour évaluer le vieillissement des parties métalliques des modules MOSFET. La caractérisation complète de l'interface soudée, intrinsèquement défectueuse et la dégradation de la métallisation pendant le vieillissement électrothermique ouvrent la voie à l'amélioration possible les technologies actuelles et au développement potentiel de nouveaux procédés.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this study, microstructural features direct metal laser melted (DMLM) aluminium–silicon-magnesium (AlSi10Mg) are investigated using advanced transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution TEM (HRTEM). The focus is on post-processing by ECAP (Equal Channel Angular Pressing) and its effects on grain refinement, stacking fault formation and dislocation accumulation. In addition, the strength enhancing role of stacking faults is for the first time quantified. The results show that ECAP can increase the yield strength from 294 to 396 MPa, while the elongation increases from 2.4% to 6%. These results show that ECAP processing offers a new approach for producing AlSi10Mg products with improved strength and ductility.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The development of advanced energy materials is critical for the safety and efficiency of next-generation nuclear energy systems. Aluminum alloys present a compelling option due to their excellent neutronic properties, notably a low thermal neutron absorption cross-section. However, their historically poor high-temperature performance has limited their use in commercial power reactors. This makes them prime candidates for specialized, lower-temperature but high-radiation environments, such as research reactors, spent fuel storage systems, and spallation neutron sources. In these applications, mitigating radiation damage—particularly swelling and embrittlement from helium produced during irradiation—remains a paramount challenge. Grain Boundary Engineering (GBE) is a potent strategy to mitigate radiation damage by increasing the fraction of low-energy Coincident Site Lattice (CSL) boundaries. These interfaces act as effective sinks for radiation-induced point defects (vacancies and self-interstitials), suppressing their accumulation and subsequent clustering into damaging dislocation loops and voids. By controlling the defect population, GBE can substantially reduce macroscopic effects like volumetric swelling and embrittlement, enhancing material performance in harsh radiation environments. In this article we evaluate the efficacy of GBE in an AlSi10Mg alloy, a candidate material for nuclear applications. Samples were prepared via KOBO extrusion, with a subset undergoing subsequent annealing to produce varied initial grain sizes and grain boundary character distributions. This allows for a direct comparison of how these microstructural features influence the material’s response to helium ion irradiation, which simulates damage from fission and fusion reactions. The resulting post-irradiation defect structures and their interaction with the engineered grain boundary network were characterized using a combination of Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and High-Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy (HRTEM), providing crucial insights for designing next-generation, radiation-tolerant energy materials.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The majority of aluminum alloys used for laser powder bed fusion are based on the aluminum–silicon system, particularly alloys containing 7 to 12 wt.% silicon and less than 1 wt.% magnesium. Silicon has a beneficial influence on melt viscosity during casting and laser additive manufacturing and prevents the formation of cracks. This study focused on the development of a new AlSi3.5Mg2.5 alloy for laser powder bed fusion with a Mg-Si content above 1.85 wt.% Mg2Si, which is the solubility limit of the α-aluminum matrix, and a subsequent heat treatment to adjust the mechanical properties with a wide range of strength and ductility values. The characterization of the microstructure was conducted by optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and differential scanning calorimetry. The mechanical properties were determined by tensile tests and additional tight radius bending tests. The newly developed alloy was compared with AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy®. AlSi3.5Mg2.5 offers higher strength and ductility than AlSi10Mg, at comparable material costs. The mechanical properties can be adjusted in a wide range of values using a single step heat treatment. After direct ageing, the samples exhibited a ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 484 ± 1 MPa and an elongation at break of 10.5% ± 1.3%, while after soft annealing, they exhibited a UTS of 179 ± 2 MPa and an elongation at break of 25.6% ± 0.9%.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF)-processed AlSi10Mg produces highly heterogeneous microstructures, where fine α-Al cells, Si-rich networks, and melt-pool boundaries govern local mechanical behavior. Nanoindentation has emerged as a key tool for probing these variations, yet systematic understanding of the links between processing parameters, microstructure, and nano-mechanical response remains limited. This critical review examines how laser processing parameters influence local mechanical response through their impact on microstructural features. Key challenges in interpreting nanoindentation are highlighted, alongside inconsistencies in experimental protocols and reporting practices that hinder cross-study comparisons. Beyond summarizing existing findings, underexplored aspects of nanoindentation in LPBF AlSi10Mg are identified, including spatially correlated microstructure-mechanical mapping, depth-resolved measurements, and integration with advanced characterization and data-driven approaches. By synthesizing current knowledge and clarifying methodological constraints, this review positions nanoindentation not merely as a descriptive tool, but as a mechanistically informed approach for linking processing conditions, microstructural heterogeneity, and local mechanical response. These insights aim to support more rigorous interpretation of small-scale mechanical data and to guide future studies toward predictive understanding and rational process optimization in additively manufactured aluminum alloys.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This study introduces a strain-annealing approach to tailor the grain boundary characteristics of additively manufactured AlSi10Mg alloy produced by Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF). By combining KOBO extrusion and subsequent annealing treatments, we aim to increase the proportion of low-Σ coincident site lattice (CSL) grain boundaries, particularly Σ3 boundaries. Through grain boundary engineering (GBE), specifically focused on inducing a high fraction of symmetrical CSL boundaries, our approach allows for the optimization of microstructural features that inhibit defect propagation and improve material stability. Microstructural analysis using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) revealed a substantial increase in Σ3 boundaries (60° <111> twin relationship) in the early recrystallization stages of the KOBO-processed LPBF AlSi10Mg alloy, demonstrating the effectiveness of this method. The findings presented in this manuscript highlight a new strategy for advancing the microstructural characteristics of LPBF AlSi10Mg alloy, with promising implications for applications requiring high-performance materials, such as in the aerospace, nuclear, and automotive industries.

Abstract:
Heat-performance nickel-based superalloys are commonly applied in various critical industries. In this work, test samples in the form of turbine blades were manufactured by means of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) 3D technology. This research focused on comparison of the influences of various surface finishing methods. The mechanical surface post-processing of the LPBF-manufactured Inconel 718 alloy samples consisted of ultrasonic impact treatment (UIT), ultrasonic shot peening (USP), shot peening (SP), and barrel finishing (BF). The surface microrelief was evaluated using a high-precision laser profilometer, while the microstructural features were studied by light optical microscopy (LOM), scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Potentiodynamic polarization tests were also conducted to compare the surface finishing methods in terms of corrosion resistance improvement of the LPBF-manufactured 718 alloy samples. The effects of the surface microstructure and hardening intensity in combination with residual stresses and surface relief coupled with roughness profile shapes on the room temperature corrosion behavior of plastically deformed 718 alloy specimens manufactured by LPBF were studied. The corrosion rate (CR) of the LPBF-manufactured samples was reduced after post-processing: BF (~16 μm/year), USP (~15 μm/year), SP (~6.5 μm/year), and UIT (~5.5 μm/year). The experimental trends also agreed well with the theoretical trends of uniform corrosion of the studied alloy.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) shows potential in metal additive manufacturing for producing complex components. However, achieving ideal hardness and minimizing porosity poses a significant challenge. This study explores the impact of part orientation, scanning methods, and hatching distance on the hardness and porosity of AlSi10Mg alloy produced through L-PBF. Utilizing a Box–Behnken design of experiments (DOE), cubic samples were systematically produced. Hardness was quantitatively assessed using Vickers hardness tests, while porosity measurements involved 2D image analysis of polished scanning electron microscopy (SEM) samples, the porosity percentages analyzed using ImageJ software. The results demonstrate that both scanning strategy and hatching distance significantly influence hardness and porosity. The spiral scanning pattern notably enhances hardness and reduces porosity. In contrast, the bidirectional scanning strategy results in lower hardness and more pronounced porosity formations. An inverse correlation between grain size distribution and hardness was observed, with finer grain sizes leading to higher hardness values, indicating that grain refinement improves mechanical properties. Additionally, a negative relationship between hardness and porosity was established, emphasizing the importance of minimizing porosity to enhance material hardness. These findings contribute to the overall understanding of the L-PBF additive manufacturing process, providing valuable insights for optimizing material properties and ensuring the mechanical integrity of high-performance L-PBF produced metal parts.

Abstract:
We present x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy data that show that the chemisorbed oxygen previously observed to be on the surface of thin $\mathrm{Al}{\mathrm{O}}_{x}$ layers formed by room temperature thermal oxidation is bound by oxygen vacancies in the oxide. Increasing the electric field across the oxide, either by overcoating with a metallic electrode, or by electron bombardment, drives this surface chemisorbed oxygen into the vacancy sites. Due to the low bonding energies of these oxygen sites, subsequent oxygen exposures draw these ${\mathrm{O}}^{\ensuremath{-}}$ ions back to the surface, reforming chemisorbed $\mathrm{O}_{2}{}^{\ensuremath{-}}$. $\mathrm{Al}∕\mathrm{Al}{\mathrm{O}}_{x}∕\mathrm{Al}$ tunnel junctions incorporating electron-bombarded $\mathrm{Al}{\mathrm{O}}_{x}$ barriers show a significant reduction in the low-frequency junction resistance noise level at $4.2\phantom{\rule{0.3em}{0ex}}\mathrm{K}$.

Abstract:
Thickness dramatically affects the functionality of coatings. Accordingly, the techniques in use to determine the thickness are of utmost importance for coatings research and technology. In this review, we analyse some of the most appropriate methods for determining the thickness of metallic coatings. In doing so, we classify the techniques into two categories: (i) destructive and (ii) non-destructive. We report on the peculiarity and accuracy of each of these methods with a focus on the pros and cons. The manuscript also covers practical issues, such as the complexity of the procedure and the time required to obtain results. While the analysis focuses most on metal coatings, many methods are also applicable to films of other materials.

Abstract:
Due to advances in EDS technology, electron microscopy techniques have become an important tool to determine the relative abundance of mineral phases. However, few studies have directly compared EDS X‐ray mineralogy with traditional techniques for assessing bulk mineralogy and elemental composition. We show that analysing a limited area (~ 0.5–3.2 mm2) of fine‐grained metal extraction samples using EDS X‐ray principal component analysis phase mapping yields results that agree within 10% with more traditional techniques for mineral phases present at greater than 5% m/m. Electron beam sensitive minerals, such as the carbonates, have poor correlations between EDS and X‐ray Diffraction (XRD) and/or WD‐XRF. Likewise, poor correlations between methods can be expected for particles that are smaller than the interaction volume of the electron beam (~ 1.5 µm); this strongly affected the phyllosilicates. One strength of EDS phase mapping is that it can identify phases present below the detection limit of powder XRD (< 1%). Our results demonstrate that EDS phase mapping is sufficient to estimate bulk sample mineralogy. If polished thin sections have been prepared, this approach may save time and/or money relative to the more traditional approaches of preparing separate subsamples for XRD and/or WD‐XRF.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000000

From text 'gauzzi2020electronbackscatterdiffraction pages 7-9'.

T Gauzzi, MCC de Souza, and GC Stumpf. Electron backscatter diffraction (ebsd) sample preparation revisited: integrating traditional methods and new techniques in the last three decades. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt supports the view that ion milling can remove or avoid residual polishing products at the sample surface: it is described as more efficient than mechanical polishing with colloidal silica specifically because it “does not produce residues.” However, the passage does not directly demonstrate chemical removal of pre-existing colloidal-silica residue, nor does it discuss EDS accuracy or contamination measurements after ion milling. It reports benefits primarily for EBSD, especially improved high-resolution Kikuchi patterns. The final abrasive choice is presented in the context of vibratory polishing for ductile metals: either colloidal silica (0.02 µm) or colloidal alumina (0.05 µm) may be used, and the process is said to minimize crystalline deformation and stress. No comparison is provided between silica and alumina regarding residual contamination, elemental EDS accuracy, detector artifacts, or whether subsequent ion milling makes their effects equivalent. Thus, the excerpt indicates that ion milling is a low-residue finishing method and that both abrasives can be used for EBSD preparation, but it does not establish whether abrasive selection matters for EDS accuracy after ion milling.


---

## pqac-00000001

From text 'remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 19-21'.

G. Rémond, C. Nockolds, M. Phillips, and C. Roques-carmes. Implications of polishing techniques in quantitative x-ray microanalysis. Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 107:639-662, Nov 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.052, doi:10.6028/jres.107.052. This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not directly address ion milling as a method for removing colloidal-silica residue, so it cannot establish whether ion milling fully eliminates that residue. It also does not provide a direct experiment comparing colloidal silica and alumina as final abrasives specifically after ion milling, nor does it report EDS accuracy before and after such treatment. It does indicate that the final polishing method matters for the specimen’s near-surface condition: colloidal-silica polishing is described as chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP), and CMP generally produces a thinner amorphous layer and shallower subsurface damage than purely mechanical polishing with quarter-micron diamond. The article further emphasizes that quantitative x-ray data can vary with polishing and instrumental parameters even after an optically polished surface is achieved. Thus, the excerpt supports the general conclusion that final-abrasive choice can affect EDS through surface damage, amorphous layers, roughness, and possible surface reaction products, but it does not support a specific conclusion about the relative EDS accuracy of colloidal silica versus alumina after ion milling.


---

## pqac-00000002

From text 'presley2016theformationof pages 34-41'.

M Presley. The formation of amorphous and crystalline damage in metallic and semiconducting materials under gallium ion irradiation. Unknown journal, 2016.

The excerpt does not directly examine colloidal silica residue from metallographic polishing or compare colloidal silica with alumina as final abrasives, so it cannot establish whether ion milling completely removes such residue or whether the abrasive choice affects EDS accuracy. It does, however, indicate that ion milling can produce redeposition and ion-beam mixing, creating an amorphous surface layer that may contain both directly damaged material and redeposited material. In the FeAl-WC example, variable EDX signals were attributed to redeposition, demonstrating that material introduced or redistributed during preparation can affect compositional measurements. The excerpt further states that low-keV cleaning did not reduce the redeposition layer in that study, although cross-sectional cleaning is generally reported to reduce redeposition and amorphous-layer thickness. Thus, ion milling should not automatically be assumed to remove polishing residues without trace or to yield residue-independent EDS results. A direct answer about silica versus alumina requires a source specifically testing those residues and final-polishing conditions.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Thin films have become indispensable in shaping the landscape of modern and future technologies, offering versatile platforms where properties can be engineered at the atomic to microscale to deliver performance unattainable with bulk materials. Historically evolving from protective coatings and optical layers, the field has advanced into a highly interdisciplinary domain that underpins innovations in microelectronics, energy harvesting, optoelectronics, sensing, and biomedical devices. In this review, a structured approach has been adopted to consolidate the fundamentals of thin film growth and the governing principles of nucleation, surface dynamics, and interface interactions, followed by an in-depth comparison of deposition strategies such as physical vapor deposition, chemical vapor deposition, atomic layer deposition (ALD), and novel solution-based techniques, highlighting their scalability, precision, and application relevance. By critically evaluating experimental studies and technological implementations, this review identifies key findings linking microstructural evolution to device performance, while also addressing the pressing challenges of stability, degradation pathways, and reliability under operational stresses. The synthesis of evidence points to the transformative role of advanced deposition controls, in situ monitoring, and emerging AI-driven optimization in overcoming current bottlenecks. Ultimately, this work concludes that thin film technologies are poised to drive the next generation of sustainable, intelligent, and multifunctional devices, with emerging frontiers such as hybrid heterostructures, quantum materials, and bio-integrated systems charting the future roadmap.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This is a review of current developments in the field of ion-plasma and beam methods of synthesis of protective and functional dielectric coatings. We give rationales for attractiveness and prospects of creating such coatings by electron-beam heating and following evaporation of dielectric targets. Forevacuum plasma electron sources, operating at elevated pressure values from units to hundreds of pascals, make it possible to exert the direct action of an electron beam on low-conductive materials. Electron-beam evaporation of aluminum oxide, boron, and silicon carbide targets is used to exemplify the particular features of electron-beam synthesis of such coatings and their parameters and characteristics.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) has significantly gained in importance and has become one of the major fabrication techniques within metal additive manufacturing. The fast cooling rates achieved in LPBF due to a relatively small melt pool on a much larger component or substrate, acting as heat sink, result in fine-grained microstructures and high oversaturation of alloying elements in the α-aluminum. Al–Si–Mg alloys thus can be effectively precipitation hardened. Moreover, the solidified material undergoes an intrinsic heat treatment, whilst the layers above are irradiated and the elevated temperature in the built chamber starts the clustering process of alloying elements directly after a scan track is fabricated. These silicon–magnesium clusters were observed with atom probe tomography in as-built samples. Similar beneficial clustering behavior at higher temperatures is known from the direct-aging approach in cast samples, whereby the artificial aging is performed immediately after solution annealing and quenching. Transferring this approach to LPBF samples as a possible post-heat treatment revealed that even after direct aging, the outstanding hardness of the as-built condition could, at best, be met, but for most instances it was significantly lower. Our investigations showed that LPBF Al–Si–Mg exhibited a high dependency on the quenching rate, which is significantly more pronounced than in cast reference samples, requiring two to three times higher quenching rate after solution annealing to yield similar hardness results. This suggests that due to the finer microstructure and the shorter diffusion path in Al–Si–Mg fabricated by LPBF, it is more challenging to achieve a metastable oversaturation necessary for precipitation hardening. This may be especially problematic in larger components.
