Abstract:
Tailoring heat treatments for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) processed materials is critical to ensure superior and repeatable material properties for high-end applications. This tailoring requires in-depth understanding of the LPBF-processed material. Therefore, the current study aims at unravelling the threefold interrelationship between the process (LPBF and heat treatment), the microstructure at different scales (macro-, meso-, micro-, and nano-scale), and the macroscopic material properties of AlSi10Mg. A similar solidification trajectory applies at different length scales when comparing the solidification of AlSi10Mg, ranging from mould-casting to rapid solidification (LPBF). The similarity in solidification trajectories triggers the reason why the Brody-Flemings cellular microsegregation solidification model could predict the cellular morphology of the LPBF as-printed microstructure. Where rapid solidification occurs at a much finer scale, the LPBF microstructure exhibits a significant grain refinement and a high degree of silicon (Si) supersaturation. This study has identified the grain refinement and Si supersaturation as critical assets of the as-printed microstructure, playing a vital role in achieving superior mechanical and thermal properties during heat treatment. Next, an electrical conductivity model could accurately predict the Si solute concentration in LPBF-processed and heat-treated AlSi10Mg and allows understanding the microstructural evolution during heat treatment. The LPBF-processed and heat-treated AlSi10Mg conditions (as-built (AB), direct-aged (DA), stress-relieved (SR), preheated (PH)) show an interesting range of superior mechanical properties (tensile strength: 300–450 MPa, elongation: 4–13%) compared to the mould-cast T6 reference condition.

M Ulitschka. Investigations on reactively driven ion beam etching procedures for improvement of optical aluminium surfaces. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt provides qualitative information relevant to differential sputtering in Al-Si or other aluminium alloys, but it does not report numerical sputtering yields for aluminium and silicon under argon-ion bombardment. It explains that sputtering yield depends strongly on ion incidence angle and energy, with the yield generally increasing toward an intermediate-angle maximum and then declining at glancing incidence because of increased ion reflection. Differences in local composition, impurities, and alloy inhomogeneity can produce locally different sputtering yields. Continued irradiation can therefore modify surface topography, particularly when unevenness, defects, or compositional variations are present. The excerpt also explicitly identifies preferential sputtering caused by inhomogeneous aluminium-alloy composition as a limitation of ion-beam processing. However, it does not discuss whether differential sputtering produces a specific surface relief in Al-Si alloys, nor does it describe effects on electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), crystallographic indexing, phase distribution, or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), including composition shifts or altered near-surface measurements. Those specific numerical yield values and characterization effects must therefore be obtained from another portion of the source or from the cited literature.

Abstract:
Abstract Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) in electron microscopy has been widely used in many research areas since it provides precise information on the chemical composition of subcellular structures that may be correlated with their high resolution images. In EDS the characteristic X-rays typical of each element are analyzed and the new detectors - an example of which we describe - allow for setting precisely the area of measurements and acquiring signals as a point analysis, as a linescan or in the image format of the desired area. Mapping of the elements requires stringent methods of sample preparation to prevent redistribution/loss of the elements as well as elimination of the risk of overlapping spectra. Both qualitative and quantitative analyses may be performed at a low probe current suitable for thin biological samples. Descriptions of preparation techniques, drawbacks and precautions necessary to obtain reliable results are provided, including data on standards, effects of specimen roughness and quantification. Data on EPMA application in different fields of biomedical and agricultural studies are reviewed. In this review we refer to recent EDS/EPMA applications in medical diagnostics, studies on air pollution and agrochemicals as well as on plant models used to monitor the environment.

Abstract:
There are two fundamental considerations in preparing samples for electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). The first one may seem obvious, but we often find it is overlooked. That is, the sample analyzed should be representative of the population from which it comes. The second is a direct result of the assumptions in the calculations used to convert x-ray intensity ratios, between the sample and standard, to concentrations. Samples originate from a wide range of sources. During their journey to being excited under the electron beam for the production of x rays there are many possibilities for sample alteration. Handling can contaminate samples by adding extraneous matter. In preparation, the various abrasives used in sizing the sample by sawing, grinding and polishing can embed themselves. The most accurate composition of a contaminated sample is, at best, not representative of the original sample; it is misleading. Our laboratory performs EPMA analysis on customer submitted samples and prepares over 250 different calibration standards including pure elements, compounds, alloys, glasses and minerals. This large variety of samples does not lend itself to mass production techniques, including automatic polishing. Our manual preparation techniques are designed individually for each sample. The use of automated preparation equipment does not lend itself to this environment, and is not included in this manuscript. The final step in quantitative electron probe microanalysis is the conversion of x-ray intensities ratios, known as the “k-ratios,” to composition (in mass fraction or atomic percent) and/or film thickness. Of the many assumptions made in the ZAF (where these letters stand for atomic number, absorption and fluorescence) corrections the localized geometry between the sample and electron beam, or takeoff angle, must be accurately known. Small angular errors can lead to significant errors in the final results. The sample preparation technique then becomes very important, and, under certain conditions, may even be the limiting factor in the analytical uncertainty budget. This paper considers preparing samples to get known geometries. It will not address the analysis of samples with irregular, unprepared surfaces or unknown geometries.

This study summarizes the principles and functions of EPMA, and the problems and difficulties, along with the recent advances in quantitative analysis of EPMA. ## pqac-00000004

From text 'nguyen2018atomicscaleinsightsinto pages 1-3'.

Lan Nguyen, Teruo Hashimoto, Dmitri N. Zakharov, Eric A. Stach, Aidan P. Rooney, Benjamin Berkels, George E. Thompson, Sarah J. Haigh, and Tim L. Burnett. Atomic-scale insights into the oxidation of aluminum. ACS applied materials & interfaces, 10 3:2230-2235, Jan 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.7b17224, doi:10.1021/acsami.7b17224. This article has 180 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt establishes that aluminum develops a stable, self-healing native oxide at room temperature, ultimately reaching a saturated thickness of a few nanometers. However, it does not provide a single numerical native-oxide thickness for an untreated room-temperature surface. It specifically warns that the oxide seen in the TEM before reoxidation had already been partly removed by electron-beam sputtering, so that measured thickness should not be interpreted as the original native-oxide thickness. The experiment instead removes the native film to create atomically pristine aluminum and then observes oxide regrowth in oxygen. The excerpt also does not discuss energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) or quantify oxygen-measurement errors at 5 kV. In general, because low-voltage EDS has a shallow electron interaction volume, a few-nanometer surface oxide can contribute disproportionately to the detected oxygen signal and bias composition estimates, especially when oxygen is quantified relative to the aluminum substrate. A precise correction requires accounting for oxide thickness, beam energy, geometry, standards, and absorption effects.

Abstract:
In this work, a simple rectangular milling technique was demonstrated to prepare needle shape atom probe tomography (APT) specimens from Al alloys by focused‐ion‐beam (FIB) milling using Ga+ ions at room temperature. Ga has high miscibility in Al owing to which electropolishing technique is preferred over Ga+ ion FIB instruments for the fabrication of APT specimens. Although, site specific sample preparation is not possible by the electropolishing technique. This led to the motivation to demonstrate a new rectangular milling technique using Ga+ FIB instrument that resulted a significant reduction of Ga+ ion impregnation into the specimens. This is attributed to the reduction of milling time (<30 s at 30 kV acceleration voltage) and the use of lower currents (<0.3 nA) compared to the conventional annular milling method. The yield of specimens during field evaporation in APT was also significantly increased from around 8 million ions to more than 86 million ions due to the avoidance of Ga+ ion embrittlement. Therefore, the currently demonstrated rectangular milling technique can be used to prepare APT specimens from Al‐alloys and obtained accurate compositions of matrix, phases, and hetero‐phase interfaces with Ga < 0.1 at%.

Abstract:
This work deals with the application of a solidification/stabilization process with the aim to obtain safe and reusable granular materials from a polluted soil and to elucidate the mechanisms involved in the retention of several heavy metals. The High Performance Solidification/Stabilization (HPSS®) process was applied to the selected contaminated soil by using both ordinary Portland cement and calcium aluminate cement, as well as several binders prepared by combining these two types of cement in different proportions. Leaching and mechanical tests were carried out to evaluate the performances of the proposed binders in the pellets produced by the HPSS® process, while XRD analysis and SEM/EDX imaging were used to investigate the phase composition and internal microstructure of the treated samples. The examination of the obtained granular materials revealed that the immobilization of Sb was mainly related to its inclusion within calcium silicate hydrates’ structure; the immobilization of Cr, Pb, Ni, Co, Zn and Tl was associated with the eluate pH and their incorporation within ettringite structure, while for Se, Cu, Ba and V, the main retention mechanism was physical encapsulation. In addition, the application of a wet conditioning process improved the materials’ performance, leading to granules always satisfying the Italian regulatory requirements for reuse. The findings obtained in this study were useful to better elucidate the mechanisms involved in the retention of heavy metals by several binders, contributing to the development of sustainable management strategies for contaminated soils and sediments through their transformation into reusable materials.

Abstract:
This study explores the use of Electric Arc Furnace (EAF) slag as a sustainable alternative raw material in cement clinker production. The research demonstrates the synthesis of ferrite-rich clinker using EAF slag, achieving a clinker composition of 47% alite, 32% ferrite, and 20% belite while replacing 20% of clinker raw materials i.e. limestone, iron and silica source. The hydration behavior and influence of carbonation curing on the reactivity of the ferrite phase were assessed. Results show that the addition of 5% gypsum to the clinker enhanced the hydration rate of alite and ferrite phases, promoting the formation of portlandite, C-S-H and ettringite as the major hydration phases. Typical of ferrite-rich cement, Fe/Al-rich siliceous hydrogarnet was also identified as secondary hydration products of the ferrite phase, formed as a result of the reaction of katoite (formed from ferrite dissolution) with dissolved silica. However, prolonged carbonation exposure led to a decrease in the formation of the hydrogarnet and the decomposition of ettringite, but the mortar’s strength increased with increasing calcium carbonate formation. ## pqac-00000027

From text 'viguier2001heatingoftem pages 7-9'.

B. Viguier and A. Mortensen. Heating of tem specimens during ion milling. Ultramicroscopy, 87 3:123-33, Apr 2001. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0304-3991(00)00095-4, doi:10.1016/s0304-3991(00)00095-4. This article has 38 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly documents substantial heating of aluminum-alloy TEM specimens during argon ion milling at 5 kV, which is within the 4–6 kV range in the question. With a DuoMill steel holder, 5 kV and a 15° incidence angle produced temperatures above 673 K in some specimens; the table records 673 K for 3 of 6 discs. Changing to a copper-legged holder under the same nominal conditions reduced the observed temperature to about 573 K for 3 of 4 samples. At 5 kV and 8°, no microstructural change was detected in some samples, consistent with lower temperatures, while the table reports approximately 573 K for steel-mounted samples. The results show that heating depends strongly on holder thermal conductivity, beam incidence angle, and beam-current stability. The authors estimate a 200 K temperature rise associated with interfacial heat-transfer resistance and conclude that the largest rise occurs in poorly conducting holder legs and at interfaces. The excerpt does not test or explicitly assess liquid-nitrogen cooling, so it cannot establish that LN2 cooling is necessary. It does demonstrate that room-temperature ion milling at ordinary 5 kV conditions can cause serious heating artifacts in aluminum alloys; cooling or improved thermal conduction may therefore be needed when preserving the solutionized microstructure is essential.

## pqac-00000028

The excerpt reports that TEM specimens can reach peak temperatures around 650 K during ion milling under conventional metallographic milling conditions. Earlier studies showed substantial variability, with temperature increases ranging from less than 100 K to more than 400 K for nominally equivalent thinning procedures. The provided pages do not explicitly identify argon ion energies of 4–6 kV, so the 650 K value should be treated as representative of conventional conditions rather than as a voltage-specific measurement. For aluminum alloys, heating is potentially significant enough to alter microstructural features and create artifacts, particularly in two-phase materials such as aluminum-based metal-matrix composites. Liquid-nitrogen cooling is not universally a necessary or reliable solution: although cooled stages are commonly used when heating is a concern, the authors explain that significant cooling or heating excursions in two-phase materials can generate thermal-expansion-misfit stresses and modify dislocation structures. They therefore state that liquid-nitrogen cooling does not provide an acceptable remedy for such materials. The study instead emphasizes controlling heat flow through the specimen holder legs and interfaces. For single-phase aluminum alloys, the excerpt does not establish that liquid nitrogen is always required; necessity depends on the alloy, microstructure, milling conditions, and sensitivity to thermally activated changes.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'dankhazi2015ebsdsamplepreparation pages 3-6'.

Zoltán Dankházi, Szilvia Kalácska, Adrienn Baris, Gábor Varga, Zsolt Radi, and Károly Havancsák. Ebsd sample preparation: high energy ar ion milling. Materials Science Forum, 812:309-314, Feb 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.4028/www.scientific.net/msf.812.309, doi:10.4028/www.scientific.net/msf.812.309. This article has 9 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt supports a comparison in which planar, shallow-angle broad Ar-ion milling is advantageous for preparing an existing roughly polished surface for high-quality EBSD. At approximately 6–8° incidence, it removes the mechanically deformed or amorphous surface layer, improves EBSD image quality, and requires relatively short treatment times; for Cu, the recommended duration is 6–8 minutes, with material-dependent values listed for Al, Ni, Fe, and steel. Milling should stop near the beginning of IQ saturation because extended processing causes surface coarsening, roughness, and potentially cratering, which are disadvantages for both EBSD quality and surface-sensitive EDS. Cross-section or slope-cut mode is advantageous when the original surface contains a thick mechanically induced amorphous layer that planar polishing cannot readily remove, or when a newly exposed subsurface is needed. It can produce a substantial section (up to 200 µm depth in 2 hours), enabling examination of internal structure. However, cross-section milling is slower and high-energy cutting generates redeposited/backsputtered material that forms an amorphous layer and blurs Kikuchi patterns. A subsequent low-energy Ar cleaning step was required to obtain a usable EBSD map. The excerpt does not directly discuss EDS performance, but the reported roughening, redeposition, and surface-layer effects would also be relevant to EDS accuracy and spatial resolution.

Venables and Harland were the ﬁrst to investigate electron backscatter Kikuchi patterns

are indexed automatically by the computer, resulting in colour being displayed on the

men [7].
   The EBSD technique is a very young technique and a very challenging one in that
sense that it requires major computing capacity, or before that was available, major
human power for the indexing of each pattern. Just for the sake of comparison, using
the ﬁrst computer-aided indexing, the operator had to select three lines at each pattern,
before the indexing could be done by the computer. The orientation maps to be shown
in this work consist of 200   200 = 40000 points.  If we assume indexing one point               ×
takes 5 seconds on average, one map would take 200000 seconds = 56 hours to produce.
These days we are lucky in that powerful computers and well written algorithms are
available to reduce the duration of one mapping (as mentioned above) to less than 15
minutes. However, we should remember that what we can do now by just one click,

                                  2KITTI RATTER                                        1  INTRODUCTION


others worked for for years (not only in the case of EBSD).
   The crucial part of the sample for the purpose of the EBSD investigation is the
surface, since the information we get comes from the upper 10 nanometer thick region
of the specimen. The surface has to be perfectly clean, there cannot be an amorphous
covering on it. If there is, either no or a faded diffraction pattern is recorded. Besides,
it has to be effectively smoothed, because of shadowing effects. The usual diamond
polishing is out of the question, because it can deform the grains on top and this induced
stress causes the diffuseness of the diffraction patterns. It has been suggested to polish
with colloidal silica for hours. When we attempted this, we could ﬁnd residual polishing
material in the grains of the sample. We also tried to prepare the surface using electro-
polishing, but we were unable to see any Kikuchi bands.
   The requirements for surface quality is very similar to what is expected in the case
of a transmission electron microscopy sample, the difference being that only one side of
the specimen is important. This similarity gave us the idea to try a device that has proven
trustworthy when preparing TEM samples: the Gentle Mill low enery argon ion polisher.
This instrument was purposely designed for the ﬁnal polishing of TEM samples by an
internationally successful company, Technoorg Linda Ltd. Co. They provided us with
an instrument to try its qualities in this area and if successful, preparing a protocol for
fast surface preparation.
   Besides probing the properties of Gentle Mill, we also used the built-in focused ion
beam system in our microscope. One of the reasons for this was that after surface prepa-
ration with the Gentle Mill, the sample had to be moved from instrument to instrument.
There can be sensitive samples that do not prefer to be transferred. With an efﬁcient
protocol, these samples can be prepared inside the microscope chamber and only stage
movements are required before the EBSD investigation can take place.
   This work is divided into two parts. In the ﬁrst part, the instruments and the meth-
ods are described. Staring with an introduction to the scanning electron microscopes
and focused ion beam systems, pointing out the speciﬁcations of our system.  In the
following chapter, the working principle of the Gentle Mill is described, then a sim-
ple model for ion sputtering is given. After the instrument descriptions, the theory of
electron backscatter diffraction is reviewed, ﬁrst with the kinematical theory, then, after
realizing that this approximation is not valid, the main ideas of dynamic theory are ex-
plained. When the theory is understood, we turn to the actual instrumentation of EBSD

    In the second part, our measurements and results are discussed, starting with the
data where FIB was used and ﬁnishing with those where Gentle Mill was employed.
The conclusion points out our main results and plots our plans for the future.

2.1  FEI Quanta 3D FEG Dual-Beam Scanning Electron Microscope

    In dual-beam electron microscopes, besides the electron source there is an ion source
as well. Both beams are suitable for imaging the surface of the sample, but the ion beam

by condenser lenses to a spot on the specimen. The diameter of the beam as measured on

Abstract:
Cooling Rate (CR) definitively influences the microstructure of metallic parts manufactured through various processes. Factors including cooling medium, surface area, thermal conductivity, and temperature control can influence both predicted and unforeseen impacts that then influence the results of mechanical properties. This comprehensive study explores the impact of CRs in diffusion, microstructural development, and the characterization of aluminum alloys and the influence of various manufacturing processes and post-process treatments, and it studies analytical models that can predict their effects. It examines a broad range of CRs encountered in diverse manufacturing methods, such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), directed energy deposition (DED), casting, forging, welding, and hot isostatic pressing (HIP). For example, varying CRs might result in different types of solidification and microstructural evolution in aluminum alloys, which thereby influence their mechanical properties during end use. The study further examines the effects of post-process heat treatments, including quenching, annealing, and precipitation hardening, on the microstructure and mechanical properties of aluminum alloys. It discusses numerical and analytical models, which are used to predict and optimize CRs for achieving targeted material characteristics of specific aluminum alloys. Although understanding CR and its effects is crucial, there is a lack of literature on how CR affects alloy properties. This comprehensive review aims to bridge the knowledge gap through a thorough literature review of the impact of CR on microstructure and mechanical properties.

The excerpt does not provide a definitive onset temperature for Si precipitation or clustering during low-temperature aging at 150, 160, or 200 °C. For as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg, DSC shows two exothermic peaks, approximately at 250 °C and 300 °C. The text reports that the peak assignment is debated: one interpretation attributes the first peak to precipitation of β-Mg2Si in the metastable β''-Mg5Si6 form and the second to diffusional Si processes in the Al matrix, while other studies report the opposite assignment. In-situ X-ray diffraction indicates that Si remains very fine and diffuse up to approximately 275 °C; above this temperature, additional Si reflections appear, increase in intensity, and sharpen, consistent with Si rejection from the supersaturated Al lattice, increasing Si volume fraction, and crystallite coarsening. Therefore, based on this excerpt, 250 °C is the lower DSC peak associated in some interpretations with precipitation-related reactions, while clear XRD evidence for substantial Si precipitation/coarsening begins above roughly 275 °C. The excerpt contains no direct data describing what specifically occurs at 150 °C, 160 °C, or 200 °C, so those aging conditions cannot be assigned a precise Si-precipitation response from this source alone.

function.arguments: {"plan_objective_id": 1, "updated_plan_objective_json": "{\"id\": 1, \"objective\": \"Search for literature on colloidal silica residue removal by ion milling and its effect on EDS accuracy (Assumptions 1-3)\", \"rationale\": \"These three assumptions are interrelated.\", \"status\": \"completed\", \"result\": \"Literature supports that ion milling avoids residues (Gauzzi 2020) and that colloidal silica polishing affects EDS/EPMA k-ratios at low voltage (R\u00e9mond 2002, Al K\u03b1 ratio = 1.058 at 5 keV after CS polishing). However no study directly tests whether ion milling fully removes pre-existing CS residue for EDS equivalence. Silica particles trapped in pores degrade EBSD indexing (Ajantiwalay 2019). Ion milling can cause redeposition.\", \"evaluation\": \"Sufficient evidence gathered for assumptions 1-3.\"}"}
function.name: update_plan

function.arguments: {"plan_objective_id": 2, "updated_plan_objective_json": "{\"id\": 2, \"objective\": \"Search for literature on differential sputtering of Al-Si alloys and milling artifacts (Assumption 4)\", \"rationale\": \"Need to assess whether preferential sputtering creates relief.\", \"status\": \"completed\", \"result\": \"Literature confirms compositional inhomogeneity in alloys leads to preferential sputtering and surface roughness (Ulitschka 2020, Barber 1993, Nowak 2021). Specific Al vs Si yield data not found in retrieved papers, but both SRIM and literature indicate different yields. Extended milling causes roughening (Dankh\u00e1zi 2015).\", \"evaluation\": \"Sufficient evidence.\"}"}
function.name: update_plan

function.arguments: {"plan_objective_id": 3, "updated_plan_objective_json": "{\"id\": 3, \"objective\": \"Search for literature on Ar implantation and ion damage effects on EDS and EBSD in aluminum alloys (Assumption 5)\", \"rationale\": \"Ar implantation depth and damage layer thickness.\", \"status\": \"completed\", \"result\": \"Ar damage layer is a few nm at 4-6 kV. Literature indicates this is generally acceptable for EBSD (Dankh\u00e1zi 2015, Fang 2022). EDS interaction volume at 5-15 kV is much deeper than few-nm damage. No specific Al Ar-implantation EDS bias study found.\", \"evaluation\": \"Sufficient evidence.\"}"}
function.name: update_plan

function.arguments: {"plan_objective_id": 4, "updated_plan_objective_json": "{\"id\": 4, \"objective\": \"Search for literature on beam heating during ion milling and effects on metastable LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure (Assumption 6)\", \"rationale\": \"Critical risk identified.\", \"status\": \"completed\", \"result\": \"TEM specimen temperatures can reach 400\u00b0C (673 K) during 5 kV Ar milling (Viguier 2001). BIB milling produces heating to at least 370\u00b0C (Ishitani 1996). Si precipitation DSC onset ~185-250\u00b0C, significant above ~275\u00b0C. Direct aging at 150-170\u00b0C already affects precipitation. This is a MAJOR RISK: ion milling can exceed Si precipitation threshold. Phenolic mount outgassing also a concern.\", \"evaluation\": \"Very strong evidence that Assumption 6 is CONTRADICTED.\"}"}
function.name: update_plan

function.arguments: {"plan_objective_id": 5, "updated_plan_objective_json": "{\"id\": 5, \"objective\": \"Search for literature on skipping vibratory polishing and going directly to ion milling (Assumption 7)\", \"rationale\": \"Need to assess whether ion milling can adequately remove deformation from coarser mechanical polishing.\", \"status\": \"completed\", \"result\": \"Deformation layer from mechanical polishing is 1-100 nm (Dankh\u00e1zi 2015). BIB milling at 4-5 kV can remove it in minutes for some materials. However optimal milling time is material-specific. AA7021 study used electropolishing before milling. Skipping vibratory step is plausible but may require longer milling, increasing heating risk.\", \"evaluation\": \"Sufficient evidence.\"}"}
function.name: update_plan

function.arguments: {"plan_objective_id": 6, "updated_plan_objective_json": "{\"id\": 6, \"objective\": \"Search for literature on native oxide regrowth on Al and its effect on EDS at low kV (Assumption 8)\", \"rationale\": \"Al oxidizes rapidly.\", \"status\": \"completed\", \"result\": \"Native oxide on Al is 2-5 nm (Mozetic 2004, Coulet 2015, Nguyen 2018). Grows rapidly then self-limits. At 5 kV EDS, interaction volume ~200-400 nm, so 3-4 nm oxide contributes ~1-2% of signal depth. R\u00e9mond 2002 shows polishing affects Al K\u03b1/O K\u03b1 ratios at 5 keV. Assumption is partially supported but requires rapid loading.\", \"evaluation\": \"Sufficient evidence.\"}"}
function.name: update_plan

function.arguments: {"plan_objective_id": 7, "updated_plan_objective_json": "{\"id\": 7, \"objective\": \"Assess planar milling vs cross-section milling (Assumption 9)\", \"rationale\": \"Compare the two modes.\", \"status\": \"completed\", \"result\": \"Planar milling offers larger area (~2 mm vs ~1 mm), faster preparation, and preserves mechanical polish geometry. Cross-section mode avoids all mechanical contact artifacts but has smaller area, more redeposition, requires cleaning step (Dankh\u00e1zi 2015). Planar is generally preferred for the stated goals.\", \"evaluation\": \"Sufficient evidence.\"}"}

function.arguments:
{"answer": "## Rubber-Duck Review of LPBF AlSi10Mg Metallographic Preparation Plan

The following assessment evaluates each of the nine numbered assumptions against published literature, identifies the dominant unconsidered risk, and proposes a minimal validation experiment. A summary of verdicts is provided in the table below.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### Assumption 1 — Ion milling removes colloidal-silica residue and deformation, so abrasive choice no longer matters for EDS

**Verdict: Partially supported; the literature is largely silent on the specific claim.**

Ion milling is described as producing residue-free surfaces and yielding better Kikuchi patterns than colloidal-silica polishing (pqac-00000000). However, no retrieved study directly demonstrates that broad-beam Ar milling fully removes a pre-existing close-packed film of ~40 nm silica spheres, nor that the EDS outcome is identical regardless of whether the prior step used colloidal silica or alumina. Rémond et al. (2002) showed that colloidal-silica-polished polycrystalline alumina yielded an Al Kα intensity ratio of 1.058 at 5 keV, compared with 0.970 for 0.25 µm diamond polish on the same material; the difference diminished toward unity at 15–25 keV (pqac-00000016). This demonstrates that the final abrasive leaves a measurable near-surface signature at low voltage. Whether 20–25 min of subsequent ion milling erases that signature entirely is untested. Meanwhile, ion milling itself can cause redeposition of sputtered material (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000025), so a pre-existing silica film could in principle be redistributed rather than cleanly removed. The assumption is plausible but not validated.

### Assumption 2 — Cleaning before milling is optional once milling is used

**Verdict: Contradicted.**

The ion-milling literature makes clear that the initial surface condition strongly affects the milled topography. Barber (1993) reported that specimens not polished to a high finish before ion milling developed very rough surfaces, attributed partly to ion deflection by charging at scratches and irregularities (pqac-00000022). Ajantiwalay et al. (2019) found that silica particles remaining in pores from vibratory polishing produced poor EBSD indexing and noted that curtaining or streaking can arise from specimen topography, inhomogeneity, and foreign sites (pqac-00000023). Contamination, grain boundaries, and compositional inhomogeneity in aluminium alloys were identified as sources of etch-pit and roughness formation during ion etching (pqac-00000021). These observations support performing the 2 min water polish (or equivalent cleaning) before milling. The claim that cleaning is optional is not supported.

### Assumption 3 — Silica trapped in pores is not redeposited; avoiding pores suffices

**Verdict: Partially supported; the literature is largely silent on redeposition from pores specifically.**

Ajantiwalay et al. (2019) confirmed that silica particles become trapped in pores during vibratory polishing and degrade EBSD indexing (pqac-00000041). No retrieved publication directly demonstrates that broad-beam ion milling redeposits pore-trapped silica onto the surrounding flat surface. However, redeposition of sputtered material is a well-recognized ion-milling artifact (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000025), so the risk cannot be categorically excluded. For a porous LPBF material, keeping EDS spots away from pores is necessary but may not be sufficient; the safest approach is to minimize residue before milling.

### Assumption 4 — Differential sputtering of eutectic Si versus α-Al produces only minor relief

**Verdict: Partially supported, with important caveats.**

Preferential sputtering of compositionally inhomogeneous alloys under Ar ion bombardment is well established. Ulitschka (2020) identified preferential erosion of alloy precipitates, compositional inhomogeneity, and grain-orientation-dependent sputtering as sources of roughness in aluminium alloys (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021). Barber (1993) noted that sputtering yield varies with phase composition and incidence angle, creating topography that can include cones, hillocks, terraces, and pits (pqac-00000024). Nowak (2021) observed that intermetallic phases and precipitates in steels sputtered at different rates, resulting in non-uniform etching and relief formation (pqac-00000042). Dankházi et al. (2015) found that extended milling beyond the optimal time caused surface coarsening and roughening, and recommended stopping when EBSD image-quality (IQ) saturates (pqac-00000035). For the fine (~200–500 nm) eutectic Si network in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg, short finishing at low incidence angle and with sample rotation should keep relief within tolerable limits for 5–15 kV EDS, but no study has quantified the resulting EDS bias specifically for this microstructure.

### Assumption 5 — Ar implantation and ion damage (a few nm) do not bias EDS or significantly reduce EBSD quality

**Verdict: Supported.**

Low-energy Ar ion milling is widely employed precisely to improve EBSD pattern quality by removing mechanically damaged material (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000044). The Ar-modified layer at 4–5 kV is on the order of a few nanometres (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000010). At 5–15 kV EDS accelerating voltages, the X-ray generation depth in Al extends several hundred nanometres, so a few-nanometre damaged or implanted layer represents a negligible fraction of the analytical volume. No retrieved study documented a measurable EDS bias from Ar implantation on Al alloys. EBSD is surface-sensitive (~10 nm information depth), but the literature consistently shows improved—not degraded—pattern quality after low-kV Ar finishing (pqac-00000035). This assumption is the best supported of the nine.

### Assumption 6 — Beam heating does not alter the metastable LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure; phenolic mount is acceptable

**Verdict: CONTRADICTED — this is the critical vulnerability in the plan.**

Viguier and Mortensen (2001) measured temperatures up to 673 K (~400 °C) in aluminium-alloy 2017 TEM specimens during 5 kV Ar ion milling (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029). Even with improved thermal contact (copper-legged holders), temperatures of ~573 K (~300 °C) were recorded (pqac-00000027). Ishitani and Yaguchi (1996) reported that conventional broad-ion-beam thinning at ~5 keV can heat specimens to at least 370 °C (pqac-00000030). Barber (1993) reported near-surface temperature rises of 200–400 °C under normal milling conditions (pqac-00000032). These data are for thin TEM foils, but a bulk specimen in a phenolic mount with poor thermal conductivity and contact may fare no better.

The LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure is acutely sensitive to such temperatures. Bosio et al. (2021) showed that the DSC signal attributed to Si diffusion and precipitation begins near approximately 185 °C in as-built LPBF Al–Si–Mg material, with a peak at ~236 °C (pqac-00000046). Direct aging at 150–170 °C progressively consumes this precipitation potential (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000009). In-situ XRD shows clear Si rejection from the supersaturated Al matrix above ~275 °C, with increasing Si volume fraction and crystallite coarsening (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048). The isothermal activation temperature for the Si-interdiffusion/spheroidisation reaction was reported as ~273 °C (pqac-00000047).

The gap between possible milling temperatures (200–400 °C) and the onset of microstructural change (~185 °C) is dangerously narrow or negative. Without a measured stage temperature for the specific instrument, holder, beam current, and mount, it cannot be assumed that 25 min at 5/4 kV is safe. Furthermore, phenolic (Bakelite) mounts are not validated for this instrument in the retrieved literature; outgassing, poor thermal conductivity, and surface charging are recognized concerns (pqac-00000043). The IB-19530CP instrument manual or vendor data should be consulted for mount compatibility.

### Assumption 7 — The 5 h vibratory step could be skipped

**Verdict: Partially supported, but with increased risk.**

Dankházi et al. (2015) reported that mechanical polishing produces an amorphous or deformed surface layer approximately 1–100 nm thick, and that shallow-angle Ar milling can remove it; for some metals the optimal milling time was only 6–8 minutes (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000035). Gauzzi et al. (2020) noted that broad-beam milling has been applied after various polishing endpoints, including some cases with only 1 µm alumina finishing (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). However, the user's cited AA7021 study reportedly included a 30 s electropolishing step before milling, which is not the same as going directly from SiC 1200 or 1 µm alumina. Skipping the vibratory step would require longer milling to remove deeper deformation, which exacerbates the already-critical heating risk (Assumption 6). The assumption is physically plausible but practically inadvisable without temperature control.

### Assumption 8 — Native-oxide regrowth adds negligible O to 5 kV EDS

**Verdict: Partially supported; prompt loading helps but does not fully resolve the issue.**

Air-exposed aluminium develops a self-limiting native oxide of approximately 2–5 nm within seconds to minutes (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). At 5 kV, the electron interaction volume in Al is on the order of 200–400 nm deep, so a 3–4 nm oxide layer constitutes roughly 1–2% of the signal depth. However, the O Kα X-ray is generated preferentially in the near-surface region because of its low energy and short mean free path, and Rémond et al. (2002) showed that polishing-method-dependent effects on Al and O X-ray intensities are most pronounced at 5 keV and largely vanish by 15–25 keV (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). Prompt loading after ion milling reduces oxide thickness and improves reproducibility, but measured oxygen at 5 kV will always include a native-oxide contribution. For rigorous O quantification, a higher voltage (10–15 kV) or a correction based on a freshly prepared Al standard would be advisable.

### Assumption 9 — Planar milling is better than cross-section mode for these goals

**Verdict: Supported.**

Planar milling preserves the mechanically prepared section plane, provides the full ~2 mm area needed for representative LPBF microstructural analysis, and efficiently finishes the surface in a shorter time than cross-section mode. Cross-section mode avoids all mechanical contact and is therefore a powerful validation tool, but it produces a narrower strip (~1 mm), generates more redeposition, and typically requires a subsequent low-energy cleaning step to achieve good EBSD patterns (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). For routine same-face EDS + EBSD correlation, planar mode is the more practical choice, provided heating and relief are controlled.

---

### Published EDS/EPMA comparisons: ion-milled vs. mechanically polished Al or Al-Si

No published study was found that directly compares quantitative EDS or EPMA accuracy (k-ratios, analytical totals) on ion-milled versus mechanically polished Al or Al-Si alloy surfaces. Rémond et al. (2002) provide the closest relevant data, comparing colloidal-silica and diamond polishing on polycrystalline alumina and showing energy-dependent intensity-ratio differences, but they did not include an ion-milled condition (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). {"answer": "## Rubber-Duck Review of LPBF AlSi10Mg Metallographic Preparation Plan

The following assessment evaluates each of the nine numbered assumptions against published literature, identifies the dominant unconsidered risk, and proposes a minimal validation experiment. A summary of verdicts is provided in the table below.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### Assumption 1 — Ion milling removes colloidal-silica residue and deformation, so abrasive choice no longer matters for EDS

**Verdict: Partially supported; the literature is largely silent on the specific claim.**

Ion milling is described as producing residue-free surfaces and yielding better Kikuchi patterns than colloidal-silica polishing (pqac-00000000). However, no retrieved study directly demonstrates that broad-beam Ar milling fully removes a pre-existing close-packed film of ~40 nm silica spheres, nor that the EDS outcome is identical regardless of whether the prior step used colloidal silica or alumina. Rémond et al. (2002) showed that colloidal-silica-polished polycrystalline alumina yielded an Al Kα intensity ratio of 1.058 at 5 keV, compared with 0.970 for 0.25 µm diamond polish on the same material; the difference diminished toward unity at 15–25 keV (pqac-00000016). This demonstrates that the final abrasive leaves a measurable near-surface signature at low voltage. Whether 20–25 min of subsequent ion milling erases that signature entirely is untested. Meanwhile, ion milling itself can cause redeposition of sputtered material (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000025), so a pre-existing silica film could in principle be redistributed rather than cleanly removed. The assumption is plausible but not validated.

### Assumption 2 — Cleaning before milling is optional once milling is used

**Verdict: Contradicted.**

The ion-milling literature makes clear that the initial surface condition strongly affects the milled topography. Barber (1993) reported that specimens not polished to a high finish before ion milling developed very rough surfaces, attributed partly to ion deflection by charging at scratches and irregularities (pqac-00000022). Ajantiwalay et al. (2019) found that silica particles remaining in pores from vibratory polishing produced poor EBSD indexing and noted that curtaining or streaking can arise from specimen topography, inhomogeneity, and foreign sites (pqac-00000023). Contamination, grain boundaries, and compositional inhomogeneity in aluminium alloys were identified as sources of etch-pit and roughness formation during ion etching (pqac-00000021). These observations support performing the 2 min water polish (or equivalent cleaning) before milling. The claim that cleaning is optional is not supported.

### Assumption 3 — Silica trapped in pores is not redeposited; avoiding pores suffices

**Verdict: Partially supported; the literature is largely silent on redeposition from pores specifically.**

Ajantiwalay et al. (2019) confirmed that silica particles become trapped in pores during vibratory polishing and degrade EBSD indexing (pqac-00000041). No retrieved publication directly demonstrates that broad-beam ion milling redeposits pore-trapped silica onto the surrounding flat surface. However, redeposition of sputtered material is a well-recognized ion-milling artifact (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000025), so the risk cannot be categorically excluded. For a porous LPBF material, keeping EDS spots away from pores is necessary but may not be sufficient; the safest approach is to minimize residue before milling.

### Assumption 4 — Differential sputtering of eutectic Si versus α-Al produces only minor relief

**Verdict: Partially supported, with important caveats.**

Preferential sputtering of compositionally inhomogeneous alloys under Ar ion bombardment is well established. Ulitschka (2020) identified preferential erosion of alloy precipitates, compositional inhomogeneity, and grain-orientation-dependent sputtering as sources of roughness in aluminium alloys (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021). Barber (1993) noted that sputtering yield varies with phase composition and incidence angle, creating topography that can include cones, hillocks, terraces, and pits (pqac-00000024). Nowak (2021) observed that intermetallic phases and precipitates in steels sputtered at different rates, resulting in non-uniform etching and relief formation (pqac-00000042). Dankházi et al. (2015) found that extended milling beyond the optimal time caused surface coarsening and roughening, and recommended stopping when EBSD image-quality (IQ) saturates (pqac-00000035). For the fine (~200–500 nm) eutectic Si network in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg, short finishing at low incidence angle and with sample rotation should keep relief within tolerable limits for 5–15 kV EDS, but no study has quantified the resulting EDS bias specifically for this microstructure.

### Assumption 5 — Ar implantation and ion damage (a few nm) do not bias EDS or significantly reduce EBSD quality

**Verdict: Supported.**

Low-energy Ar ion milling is widely employed precisely to improve EBSD pattern quality by removing mechanically damaged material (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000044). The Ar-modified layer at 4–5 kV is on the order of a few nanometres (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000010). At 5–15 kV EDS accelerating voltages, the X-ray generation depth in Al extends several hundred nanometres, so a few-nanometre damaged or implanted layer represents a negligible fraction of the analytical volume. No retrieved study documented a measurable EDS bias from Ar implantation on Al alloys. EBSD is surface-sensitive (~10 nm information depth), but the literature consistently shows improved—not degraded—pattern quality after low-kV Ar finishing (pqac-00000035). This assumption is the best supported of the nine.

### Assumption 6 — Beam heating does not alter the metastable LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure; phenolic mount is acceptable

**Verdict: CONTRADICTED — this is the critical vulnerability in the plan.**

Viguier and Mortensen (2001) measured temperatures up to 673 K (~400 °C) in aluminium-alloy 2017 TEM specimens during 5 kV Ar ion milling (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029). Even with improved thermal contact (copper-legged holders), temperatures of ~573 K (~300 °C) were recorded (pqac-00000027). Ishitani and Yaguchi (1996) reported that conventional broad-ion-beam thinning at ~5 keV can heat specimens to at least 370 °C (pqac-00000030). Barber (1993) reported near-surface temperature rises of 200–400 °C under normal milling conditions (pqac-00000032). These data are for thin TEM foils, but a bulk specimen in a phenolic mount with poor thermal conductivity and contact may fare no better.

The LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure is acutely sensitive to such temperatures. Bosio et al. (2021) showed that the DSC signal attributed to Si diffusion and precipitation begins near approximately 185 °C in as-built LPBF Al–Si–Mg material, with a peak at ~236 °C (pqac-00000046). Direct aging at 150–170 °C progressively consumes this precipitation potential (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000009). In-situ XRD shows clear Si rejection from the supersaturated Al matrix above ~275 °C, with increasing Si volume fraction and crystallite coarsening (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048). The isothermal activation temperature for the Si-interdiffusion/spheroidisation reaction was reported as ~273 °C (pqac-00000047).

The gap between possible milling temperatures (200–400 °C) and the onset of microstructural change (~185 °C) is dangerously narrow or negative. Without a measured stage temperature for the specific instrument, holder, beam current, and mount, it cannot be assumed that 25 min at 5/4 kV is safe. Furthermore, phenolic (Bakelite) mounts are not validated for this instrument in the retrieved literature; outgassing, poor thermal conductivity, and surface charging are recognized concerns (pqac-00000043). The IB-19530CP instrument manual or vendor data should be consulted for mount compatibility.

### Assumption 7 — The 5 h vibratory step could be skipped

**Verdict: Partially supported, but with increased risk.**

Dankházi et al. (2015) reported that mechanical polishing produces an amorphous or deformed surface layer approximately 1–100 nm thick, and that shallow-angle Ar milling can remove it; for some metals the optimal milling time was only 6–8 minutes (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000035). Gauzzi et al. (2020) noted that broad-beam milling has been applied after various polishing endpoints, including some cases with only 1 µm alumina finishing (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). However, the user's cited AA7021 study reportedly included a 30 s electropolishing step before milling, which is not the same as going directly from SiC 1200 or 1 µm alumina. Skipping the vibratory step would require longer milling to remove deeper deformation, which exacerbates the already-critical heating risk (Assumption 6). The assumption is physically plausible but practically inadvisable without temperature control.

### Assumption 8 — Native-oxide regrowth adds negligible O to 5 kV EDS

**Verdict: Partially supported; prompt loading helps but does not fully resolve the issue.**

Air-exposed aluminium develops a self-limiting native oxide of approximately 2–5 nm within seconds to minutes (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). At 5 kV, the electron interaction volume in Al is on the order of 200–400 nm deep, so a 3–4 nm oxide layer constitutes roughly 1–2% of the signal depth. However, the O Kα X-ray is generated preferentially in the near-surface region because of its low energy and short mean free path, and Rémond et al. (2002) showed that polishing-method-dependent effects on Al and O X-ray intensities are most pronounced at 5 keV and largely vanish by 15–25 keV (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). Prompt loading after ion milling reduces oxide thickness and improves reproducibility, but measured oxygen at 5 kV will always include a native-oxide contribution. For rigorous O quantification, a higher voltage (10–15 kV) or a correction based on a freshly prepared Al standard would be advisable.

### Assumption 9 — Planar milling is better than cross-section mode for these goals

**Verdict: Supported.**

Planar milling preserves the mechanically prepared section plane, provides the full ~2 mm area needed for representative LPBF microstructural analysis, and efficiently finishes the surface in a shorter time than cross-section mode. Cross-section mode avoids all mechanical contact and is therefore a powerful validation tool, but it produces a narrower strip (~1 mm), generates more redeposition, and typically requires a subsequent low-energy cleaning step to achieve good EBSD patterns (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). For routine same-face EDS + EBSD correlation, planar mode is the more practical choice, provided heating and relief are controlled.

---

### Published EDS/EPMA comparisons: ion-milled vs. mechanically polished Al or Al-Si

No published study was found that directly compares quantitative EDS or EPMA accuracy (k-ratios, analytical totals) on ion-milled versus mechanically polished Al or Al-Si alloy surfaces. Rémond et al. (2002) provide the closest relevant data, comparing colloidal-silica and diamond polishing on polycrystalline alumina and showing energy-dependent intensity-ratio differences, but they did not include an ion-milled condition (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). Geller and Engle (2002) discuss general preparation effects on EPMA accuracy but not ion milling specifically (pqac-00000017). This represents a genuine gap in the published literature.

---

### Biggest risk not considered

The dominant unconsidered risk is **thermal alteration of the metastable as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure by beam heating during broad-beam Ar ion milling**. Measured specimen temperatures during 5 kV milling can reach 300–400 °C (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030), while DSC exothermic events associated with Si precipitation in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg begin near ~185 °C (pqac-00000046) and significant Si rejection/coarsening occurs above ~275 °C (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). A phenolic mount compounds the problem through poor thermal conductivity, potential outgassing, and uncertain mechanical stability under vacuum and local heating. If the sample reaches even 200 °C during milling, the cellular Si network and Si supersaturation that define the as-built condition may be irreversibly altered before a single measurement is made. This would silently corrupt both EDS (apparent Si redistribution) and EBSD (recrystallization, grain-boundary migration) data.

### Smallest experiment to test it

**Tape a K-type thermocouple to the polished face of a sacrificial as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg sample (mounted in the same phenolic resin), run the planned 5 kV / 20 min + 4 kV / 5 min milling protocol, and record the temperature versus time.** If the peak surface temperature exceeds ~160 °C, the risk is confirmed. As a second check, compare DSC heating scans (5 °C min⁻¹, 25–350 °C) of a small chip extracted from the milled region and from an unmilled region of the same sample. A diminished or shifted first exothermic peak (expected near 236 °C) would indicate that ion-beam heating consumed part of the precipitation potential during preparation, confirming microstructural alteration. This single thermocouple experiment costs one sacrificial sample and ~30 min of instrument time, and would definitively answer whether the current plan can preserve the as-built condition or whether stage cooling is mandatory."}

state.question:
Rubber-duck review of a metallographic preparation plan. Please challenge it. For each numbered assumption below, say whether the published literature supports it, contradicts it, or is silent, with citations and numbers where available. Then name the biggest risk we have not considered, and the smallest experiment that would test it.

Context. Material: laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) AlSi10Mg in the as-built condition (fine cellular eutectic Si network, Si-supersaturated Al, some gas and lack-of-fusion pores); later, other Al alloys, some of them Si-free. Goals: quantitative SEM-EDS at 5-15 kV (Al, Si, Mg, O and minor elements) and EBSD on the same polished face. Equipment: a rotary grinder/polisher, a Buehler VibroMet 2 vibratory polisher, and a JEOL IB-19530CP-type broad argon-ion "cross section polisher" that is also used for planar (flat) surface milling of an area about 2 mm across. Samples are ~1 cm pieces hot-mounted in phenolic (Bakelite).

Current plan: SiC paper 320, 400, 600, 800, 1200 (US CAMI grades) -> 1 um alumina on a flock cloth -> 0.05 um alkaline colloidal silica on the VibroMet 2 for about 5 h -> 2 min on a clean soft pad with distilled water only at 40 rpm -> rinse, ethanol/methanol, dry -> broad-beam Ar ion planar milling (copying a recent study on AA7021 sheet: 5 kV for 20 min, then 4 kV for 5 min) -> SEM-EDS and EBSD.

Assumptions to test:
1. Ion milling after the silica step removes both the colloidal-silica residue (an earlier sample carried a close-packed film of ~40 nm silica spheres) and the residual deformation layer, so the choice of final abrasive (colloidal silica vs 0.05 um alumina) no longer matters for EDS accuracy.
2. Particles or films left on the surface before milling do not cause milling artifacts (masking, cones, ripples), so cleaning before milling (the 2 min water polish, per Maleki et al. 2023, Additive Manufacturing Letters 5:100122) is optional once milling is used.
3. Silica trapped in pores is not removed by milling but is not redeposited onto the surrounding surface either; keeping EDS spots away from pores is enough.
4. Differential sputtering of eutectic Si versus the alpha-Al matrix under 4-6 kV Ar ions at low incidence angle produces only minor relief that does not bias EDS quantification at 5-15 kV or degrade EBSD.
5. Ar implantation and ion damage (a few nm) do not bias EDS and do not significantly reduce EBSD pattern quality on aluminum.
6. Beam heating during ~25 min of milling at 5 kV does not alter the metastable as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure (Si precipitation from supersaturated Al, coarsening or spheroidization of the Si network), so a cooled stage is unnecessary. The phenolic mount is not a problem in the mill (outgassing, charging, heating).
7. The 5 h vibratory step could be skipped: going from 1 um alumina (or even from SiC 1200) straight to ion milling would still give EBSD-quality, residue-free surfaces, because 20-25 min of 4-5 kV planar milling removes the deformed layer left by 1 um alumina on Al-Si. (The AA7021 study also electropolished for 30 s before milling.)
8. After milling, native-oxide regrowth during transfer to the SEM adds negligible O to 5 kV EDS; loading promptly is enough.
9. Planar milling of the mechanically polished face is a better route for these goals than the same tool's cross-section mode (a ~1 mm wide ion-cut face perpendicular to the mount surface, with no abrasive contact).

Also: is there any published comparison of quantitative EDS or EPMA accuracy (k-ratios, analytical totals) on ion-milled versus mechanically polished Al or Al-Si alloy surfaces?

However, no retrieved study directly demonstrates that broad-beam Ar milling fully removes a pre-existing close-packed film of ~40 nm silica spheres, nor that the EDS outcome is identical regardless of whether the prior step used colloidal silica or alumina. Rémond et al. (2002) showed that colloidal-silica-polished polycrystalline alumina yielded an Al Kα intensity ratio of 1.058 at 5 keV, compared with 0.970 for 0.25 µm diamond polish on the same material; the difference diminished toward unity at 15–25 keV (remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 19-21). This demonstrates that the final abrasive leaves a measurable near-surface signature at low voltage. Whether 20–25 min of subsequent ion milling erases that signature entirely is untested. Meanwhile, ion milling itself can cause redeposition of sputtered material (presley2016theformationof pages 34-41), so a pre-existing silica film could in principle be redistributed rather than cleanly removed. The assumption is plausible but not validated.

### Assumption 2 — Cleaning before milling is optional once milling is used

**Verdict: Contradicted.**

The ion-milling literature makes clear that the initial surface condition strongly affects the milled topography. Barber (1993) reported that specimens not polished to a high finish before ion milling developed very rough surfaces, attributed partly to ion deflection by charging at scratches and irregularities (barber1993radiationdamagein pages 10-12). Ajantiwalay et al. (2019) found that silica particles remaining in pores from vibratory polishing produced poor EBSD indexing and noted that curtaining or streaking can arise from specimen topography, inhomogeneity, and foreign sites (ajantiwalay2019bestpracticesfor pages 5-7). Contamination, grain boundaries, and compositional inhomogeneity in aluminium alloys were identified as sources of etch-pit and roughness formation during ion etching (ulitschka2020investigationsonreactively pages 119-123). These observations support performing the 2 min water polish (or equivalent cleaning) before milling. The claim that cleaning is optional is not supported.

### Assumption 3 — Silica trapped in pores is not redeposited; avoiding pores suffices

**Verdict: Partially supported; the literature is largely silent on redeposition from pores specifically.**

Ajantiwalay et al. (2019) confirmed that silica particles become trapped in pores during vibratory polishing and degrade EBSD indexing (ajantiwalay2019bestpracticesfor pages 5-7). No retrieved publication directly demonstrates that broad-beam ion milling redeposits pore-trapped silica onto the surrounding flat surface. However, redeposition of sputtered material is a well-recognized ion-milling artifact (presley2016theformationof pages 34-41), so the risk cannot be categorically excluded. For a porous LPBF material, keeping EDS spots away from pores is necessary but may not be sufficient; the safest approach is to minimize residue before milling.

### Assumption 4 — Differential sputtering of eutectic Si versus α-Al produces only minor relief

**Verdict: Partially supported, with important caveats.**

Preferential sputtering of compositionally inhomogeneous alloys under Ar ion bombardment is well established. Ulitschka (2020) identified preferential erosion of alloy precipitates, compositional inhomogeneity, and grain-orientation-dependent sputtering as sources of roughness in aluminium alloys (ulitschka2020investigationsonreactively pages 21-24, ulitschka2020investigationsonreactively pages 119-123). Barber (1993) noted that sputtering yield varies with phase composition and incidence angle, creating topography that can include cones, hillocks, terraces, and pits (barber1993radiationdamagein pages 5-8). Nowak (2021) observed that intermetallic phases and precipitates in steels sputtered at different rates, resulting in non-uniform etching and relief formation (nowak2021theuseof pages 2-7). Dankházi et al. (2015) found that extended milling beyond the optimal time caused surface coarsening and roughening, and recommended stopping when EBSD image-quality (IQ) saturates (dankhazi2015ebsdsamplepreparation pages 3-6). For the fine (~200–500 nm) eutectic Si network in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg, short finishing at low incidence angle and with sample rotation should keep relief within tolerable limits for 5–15 kV EDS, but no study has quantified the resulting EDS bias specifically for this microstructure.

### Assumption 5 — Ar implantation and ion damage (a few nm) do not bias EDS or significantly reduce EBSD quality

**Verdict: Supported.**

Low-energy Ar ion milling is widely employed precisely to improve EBSD pattern quality by removing mechanically damaged material (dankhazi2015ebsdsamplepreparation pages 3-6, fang2022optimizingbroadion pages 1-6, ratter2012surfacepreparationfor pages 7-11). The Ar-modified layer at 4–5 kV is on the order of a few nanometres (dankhazi2015ebsdsamplepreparation pages 1-3, presley2016theformationof pages 41-46). At 5–15 kV EDS accelerating voltages, the X-ray generation depth in Al extends several hundred nanometres, so a few-nanometre damaged or implanted layer represents a negligible fraction of the analytical volume. No retrieved study documented a measurable EDS bias from Ar implantation on Al alloys. EBSD is surface-sensitive (~10 nm information depth), but the literature consistently shows improved—not degraded—pattern quality after low-kV Ar finishing (dankhazi2015ebsdsamplepreparation pages 3-6). This assumption is the best supported of the nine.

### Assumption 6 — Beam heating does not alter the metastable LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure; phenolic mount is acceptable

**Verdict: CONTRADICTED — this is the critical vulnerability in the plan.**

Viguier and Mortensen (2001) measured temperatures up to 673 K (~400 °C) in aluminium-alloy 2017 TEM specimens during 5 kV Ar ion milling (viguier2001heatingoftem pages 7-9, viguier2001heatingoftem pages 9-11). Even with improved thermal contact (copper-legged holders), temperatures of ~573 K (~300 °C) were recorded (viguier2001heatingoftem pages 7-9). Ishitani and Yaguchi (1996) reported that conventional broad-ion-beam thinning at ~5 keV can heat specimens to at least 370 °C (ishitani1996cross‐sectionalsamplepreparation pages 9-11). Barber (1993) reported near-surface temperature rises of 200–400 °C under normal milling conditions (barber1993radiationdamagein pages 8-10). The LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure is acutely sensitive to such temperatures. Bosio et al. (2021) showed that the DSC signal attributed to Si diffusion and precipitation begins near approximately 185 °C in as-built LPBF Al–Si–Mg material, with a peak at ~236 °C (bosio2021strengtheningstrategiesfor pages 3-5). In-situ XRD shows clear Si rejection from the supersaturated Al matrix above ~275 °C, with increasing Si volume fraction and crystallite coarsening (giovagnoli2021ontheprocessmicrostructureproperties pages 77-81, giovagnoli2021ontheprocessmicrostructureproperties pages 81-86). The isothermal activation temperature for the Si-interdiffusion/spheroidisation reaction was reported as ~273 °C (mehran2021onmicrostructureand pages 47-53).

The gap between possible milling temperatures (200–400 °C) and the onset of microstructural change (~185 °C) is dangerously narrow or negative. Without a measured stage temperature for the specific instrument, holder, beam current, and mount, it cannot be assumed that 25 min at 5/4 kV is safe. Furthermore, phenolic (Bakelite) mounts are not validated for this instrument in the retrieved literature; outgassing, poor thermal conductivity, and surface charging are recognized concerns (westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 5-7). The IB-19530CP instrument manual or vendor data should be consulted for mount compatibility.

### Assumption 7 — The 5 h vibratory step could be skipped

**Verdict: Partially supported, but with increased risk.**

Dankházi et al. (2015) reported that mechanical polishing produces an amorphous or deformed surface layer approximately 1–100 nm thick, and that shallow-angle Ar milling can remove it; for some metals the optimal milling time was only 6–8 minutes (dankhazi2015ebsdsamplepreparation pages 1-3, dankhazi2015ebsdsamplepreparation pages 3-6). Gauzzi et al. (2020) noted that broad-beam milling has been applied after various polishing endpoints, including some cases with only 1 µm alumina finishing (gauzzi2020electronbackscatterdiffraction pages 7-9, gauzzi2020electronbackscatterdiffractiona pages 7-9). However, the user's cited AA7021 study reportedly included a 30 s electropolishing step before milling, which is not the same as going directly from SiC 1200 or 1 µm alumina. Skipping the vibratory step would require longer milling to remove deeper deformation, which exacerbates the already-critical heating risk (Assumption 6). The assumption is physically plausible but practically inadvisable without temperature control.

### Assumption 8 — Native-oxide regrowth adds negligible O to 5 kV EDS

**Verdict: Partially supported; prompt loading helps but does not fully resolve the issue.**

Air-exposed aluminium develops a self-limiting native oxide of approximately 2–5 nm within seconds to minutes (nguyen2018atomicscaleinsightsinto pages 1-3, mozetic2004aescharacterizationof pages 1-2, coulet2015oxidationmechanismof pages 1-2, coulet2015oxidationmechanismof pages 2-3). At 5 kV, the electron interaction volume in Al is on the order of 200–400 nm deep, so a 3–4 nm oxide layer constitutes roughly 1–2% of the signal depth. However, the O Kα X-ray is generated preferentially in the near-surface region because of its low energy and short mean free path, and Rémond et al. Prompt loading after ion milling reduces oxide thickness and improves reproducibility, but measured oxygen at 5 kV will always include a native-oxide contribution. For rigorous O quantification, a higher voltage (10–15 kV) or a correction based on a freshly prepared Al standard would be advisable.

### Assumption 9 — Planar milling is better than cross-section mode for these goals

**Verdict: Supported.**

Planar milling preserves the mechanically prepared section plane, provides the full ~2 mm area needed for representative LPBF microstructural analysis, and efficiently finishes the surface in a shorter time than cross-section mode. Cross-section mode avoids all mechanical contact and is therefore a powerful validation tool, but it produces a narrower strip (~1 mm), generates more redeposition, and typically requires a subsequent low-energy cleaning step to achieve good EBSD patterns (dankhazi2015ebsdsamplepreparation pages 3-6, fang2022optimizingbroadion pages 1-6, ishitani1996cross‐sectionalsamplepreparation pages 4-6). For routine same-face EDS + EBSD correlation, planar mode is the more practical choice, provided heating and relief are controlled.

---

### Published EDS/EPMA comparisons: ion-milled vs. mechanically polished Al or Al-Si

No published study was found that directly compares quantitative EDS or EPMA accuracy (k-ratios, analytical totals) on ion-milled versus mechanically polished Al or Al-Si alloy surfaces. Rémond et al. (2002) provide the closest relevant data, comparing colloidal-silica and diamond polishing on polycrystalline alumina and showing energy-dependent intensity-ratio differences, but they did not include an ion-milled condition (remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 19-21, remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 17-19, remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 14-15). Geller and Engle (2002) discuss general preparation effects on EPMA accuracy but not ion milling specifically (geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 9-12). This represents a genuine gap in the published literature.

---

### Biggest risk not considered

The dominant unconsidered risk is **thermal alteration of the metastable as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg microstructure by beam heating during broad-beam Ar ion milling**. Measured specimen temperatures during 5 kV milling can reach 300–400 °C (viguier2001heatingoftem pages 7-9, viguier2001heatingoftem pages 9-11, ishitani1996cross‐sectionalsamplepreparation pages 9-11), while DSC exothermic events associated with Si precipitation in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg begin near ~185 °C (bosio2021strengtheningstrategiesfor pages 3-5) and significant Si rejection/coarsening occurs above ~275 °C (giovagnoli2021ontheprocessmicrostructureproperties pages 77-81, mehran2021onmicrostructureand pages 47-53, giovagnoli2021ontheprocessmicrostructureproperties pages 81-86). A phenolic mount compounds the problem through poor thermal conductivity, potential outgassing, and uncertain mechanical stability under vacuum and local heating. If the sample reaches even 200 °C during milling, the cellular Si network and Si supersaturation that define the as-built condition may be irreversibly altered before a single measurement is made. This would silently corrupt both EDS (apparent Si redistribution) and EBSD (recrystallization, grain-boundary migration) data.

### Smallest experiment to test it

**Tape a K-type thermocouple to the polished face of a sacrificial as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg sample (mounted in the same phenolic resin), run the planned 5 kV / 20 min + 4 kV / 5 min milling protocol, and record the temperature versus time.** If the peak surface temperature exceeds ~160 °C, the risk is confirmed. As a second check, compare DSC heating scans (5 °C min⁻¹, 25–350 °C) of a small chip extracted from the milled region and from an unmilled region of the same sample. A diminished or shifted first exothermic peak (expected near 236 °C) would indicate that ion-beam heating consumed part of the precipitation potential during preparation, confirming microstructural alteration. This single thermocouple experiment costs one sacrificial sample and ~30 min of instrument time, and would definitively answer whether the current plan can preserve the as-built condition or whether stage cooling is mandatory.
